PSOJ calls for improved service, pushes back on NWC increase proposal 

 Latest News, News 

October 22, 2026




 PSOJ calls for improved service, pushes back on NWC increase proposal 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Private Sector Organisation of Jamaica (PSOJ) is calling for accountability before any increase is granted to the National Water Commission (NWC) following the commission’s application for a 51 per cent tariff hike.

“The National Water Commission has a genuine financial and infrastructure problem, and we recognise the urgent need to improve Jamaica’s water supply and reliability. However, a 51 per cent tariff increase cannot be approved without clear conditions and accountability,” said Executive Director of the PSOJ Sacha Vaccianna-Riley.

Vaccianna-Riley said businesses and households are already under pressure and customers should not be expected to carry the cost of inefficiencies that remain unresolved.

She pointed to current non-revenue water issues at the facility as a point of significant concern.

“We are particularly concerned that the NWC is losing an estimated 70 per cent to 73 per cent of the water it produces through leakage and other forms of non-revenue water. The commission has also spent more than $800 million monthly on electricity. So before customers are asked to pay significantly more, there must be a clear plan to reduce these losses, improve collections and cut energy costs,” Vaccianna-Riley said.

She added that the commissions’ outstanding $21 billion GCT liability should be addressed separately rather than passed on to customers through their water bills.

“The PSOJ is therefore calling for any tariff increase to be phased and tied to measurable performance targets. That means independently verified savings, better service reliability, transparent use of capital funds and clear evidence that promised improvements are being delivered,” she said.

 DJ Tygga Ty and Charly Black Take ‘Mi Love’ to No 1 in Colombia 







DJ Tygga Ty is giving Colombia something to love.

The DJ and producer says Mi Love, his collaboration with Charly Black on the Shining Star riddim, has reached No 1 on an iTunes chart in Colombia, with the song generating 26,000 streams worldwide.

“I am feeling blessed because this is a tremendous achievement for my record label, as it is a great breakthrough in the Latin market where Charly Black has a huge following,” DJ Tygga Ty said.

The showing adds momentum to a project that also features Rytikal and Yaksta.

According to Tygga Ty, Yaksta’s release on the riddim previously reached No 1 on iTunes.

“The Shining Star riddim has generated over 38,000 streams worldwide. We will be shooting a number of music videos to amp up promotion in the markets overseas but the early feedback has been amazing,” he said.

DJ Tygga Ty’s credits include the Motif riddim, featuring Mr Vegas’ Put Me to Work, and the Apple Bag riddim, featuring Qraig of Voicemail’s Shake It. His collaborators also include Silk Boss, Singing Sweet, Rytikal and Yaksta.

Born in Florida and raised in New York, Tygga Ty now works across Rochester, Houston and Jamaica. His Houston club engagements include Lov3 and Vice, while his ties to Spanish Town’s Powasquad International keep him connected to Jamaican sound-system culture.

For him, that relationship means “family, loyalty, and respect.”

Those principles took shape during his early years helping to string up sound systems and watching artistes record dubplates. Growing up in a predominantly Black community with a Puerto Rican presence, he learned that the music came with responsibilities: respect its foundations and deliver when your turn arrives

His working philosophy remains direct.

“You only as good as your last show, and customer service is your best friend in this field of work,” said Tygga Ty.

Radio offers another test of that philosophy. He hosts an hour-long Friday programme on Rochester’s The Beat 105.5 FM, available through iHeartRadio, and has appeared on Buffalo’s WBLK and Houston’s 97.9 The Box. His radio work also includes 25-minute hip-hop mixes aimed at younger urban listeners.

“Radio also helps me work on my people skills of talking to people I may never meet and make them feel like a star through music and dialogue,” he said.

With Mi Love finding listeners in Colombia, that audience is stretching further.

“This success just shows the reach of dancehall music in the Latin market as well as global spaces that welcome dancehall and that’s a great look for the future,” said Tygga Ty.

 PAHO urges Caribbean to prepare for dengue, chikungunya rise 







WASHINGTON, United States (CMC) – The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) is urging Caribbean countries to strengthen disease surveillance and prepare health services for possible increases in dengue and chikungunya, amid renewed transmission in parts of the Americas and the anticipated intensification of the El Niño phenomenon.

In an epidemiological update issued on Wednesday, PAHO reported 1.69 million suspected dengue cases across the Americas as of mid-September, including 3,413 severe cases and 571 deaths.

Although the cumulative number of reported cases was 58 per cent lower than during the same period in 2025, the agency said the decline had not been consistent across the region.

Increases had been observed in recent weeks in the Andean, Central American and Caribbean subregions, while all four dengue virus serotypes were circulating in the Americas in 2026.

PAHO also raised concerns about chikungunya, reporting increased transmission between late 2025 and 2026, including renewed circulation in countries and territories where the virus had not been detected for several years.

As of mid-September, 213,919 suspected chikungunya cases had been reported across 20 countries in the region. Of these, 78,481 were confirmed, with 88 deaths recorded.

The agency also pointed to transmission in new areas, outbreaks outside historically affected seasons, longer periods of transmission and increased reports of more severe clinical manifestations.

PAHO is calling on countries to strengthen epidemiological, virological and entomological surveillance, expand diagnostic capacity and ensure that cases are detected early and patients receive timely care.

It also recommended stronger integrated measures to control Aedes mosquitoes, which transmit both diseases.

Health services should be prepared to respond to potential increases in cases at all levels of care, PAHO said, with particular attention to strengthening primary healthcare workers’ ability to recognise dengue warning signs early and prevent progression to severe illness.

Hospitals should also be ready to manage patients with warning signs and severe cases, the agency added.

PAHO further urged countries to improve environmental management, remove containers that collect water and encourage communities, families, local authorities and other sectors to participate actively in mosquito prevention and control.

Eliminating mosquito breeding sites remains a key measure in reducing mosquito populations, the agency said.

October 22, 2026




 No more taking out the trash at your Airbnb 







PARIS, France (AFP) — The days of having to take out the trash or wash the dishes before leaving an Airbnb are numbered as the short-term rental platform is tightening rules on what conditions hosts may impose on guests.

“Our rules regarding accommodations allow travellers to receive guidelines from hosts; however, our community has let us know that they can be confusing, restrictive, and difficult to manage,” Airbnb said Thursday to AFP.

New rules published this week that will apply to reservations made from November 20 will seek to reduce that confusion.

In particular, the new rules will generally prohibit hosts from asking guests “to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”

Hosts can still ask guests to put dirty dishes in the sink or separate trash and recyclables.

Hosts will also no longer be able to impose fines or penalties on guests. Hosts must instead must seek compensation for any damage from insurance provided through Airbnb.

 Guatemalan former cops get up to 60 year sentences in gay couple’s killings 







GUATEMALA CITY, Guatemala (AFP) — A Guatemalan court has sentenced seven former police officers to up to 60 years in prison over the “extrajudicial execution” of a gay couple, killings denounced by human rights groups as a hate crime.

Eldin Choc, 28, and Milton Santamaria, 45, were beaten, tortured and killed in April 2024 by officers making “homophobic remarks” during the incident at a police station in the town of San Andres Itzapa, prosecutor Marco Escobar told AFP.

“It is something despicable,” Judge Maria Castellanos said during the sentencing hearing.

The police chief at the time, Edy Vasquez, was sentenced Wednesday to 60 years in prison. Another former officer also received a 60-year sentence, while a third was given 30 years for committing “extrajudicial execution.”

Two female former police officers were sentenced to 11 years for dereliction of duty and discrimination for directing “homophobic remarks” at the couple, according to the ruling.

The other two defendants were sentenced to eight and 10 years in prison for charges including unlawful detention, abuse of authority, obstruction of justice and dereliction of duty.

Choc, who was Guatemalan, and Santamaria, who was Salvadoran-Canadian, had reportedly been arrested over an altercation in a shop.

The police reported the couple as having died in a traffic accident. Santamaria’s body was taken to a hospital, while Choc’s remains were found days later in a ravine with one hand mutilated.

Two firefighters have previously been sentenced to one and three years in prison after confessing, under pressure from police, that they helped cover up Santamaria being dead by the time they took him to the hospital.

“This case adds to the many other hate crimes against LGBTIQ+ people in Guatemala,” Amnesty International and other rights groups said in a joint statement.

Henry Choc, Eldin’s brother, told reporters he felt “satisfied” with the outcome, adding that “justice has been served.”

“It was important that this did not go unpunished,” Abraham Abrego, legal director of the organisation Cristosal and a plaintiff in the case, told AFP.

“This is clearly a crime motivated by prejudice,” he added.

Several activists gathered outside the courthouse holding banners with the slogan: “Homophobia kills.”

There were around 30 violent deaths of LGBTQ people in Guatemala last year, according to the Lambda Association, a Guatemalan human rights group. Hate crime is not defined under Guatemalan law.

news.title: Trump administration oversaw 980,000 deportations during first 18 months
news.text:
The US Department of
Homeland Security oversaw 980,000 deportations during ​the first
18 months of President Donald Trump's second ‌term, according to
a report published on Thursday ​in the Migration Policy Institute
think tank.

Only 20 per cent of all deportations in this period involved
individuals with a criminal conviction, the report said.

Of ‌deportations of immigrants with two or more years of US
residence, 71 per cent were of ‌people who did not have a ‌criminal
conviction, ⁠it added.

The report was authored ⁠by Marc Rosenblum, a former head
of the DHS Office of Homeland Security Statistics.

On an annual basis, total deportations ​are up from ‌the
administration of former President Joe Biden and Trump's first
term, but remained well below levels routinely observed in the
early 2000s, the report said.

Out of the 980,000 Immigration and ​Customs Enforcement and
Customs and Border Protection deportations during Trump's second
term, about 59 per cent, or ⁠580,000, were removals, 30 per cent, or 300,000,
were enforcement returns, and 11 per cent, or 110,000, were
administrative returns, the ‌report said.

Trump says his immigration crackdown and deportation drive
aim to improve domestic security.

Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due
process and free speech rights and has created an unsafe
environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have
raised ‌concerns about racial profiling.

The State Department said ​on Tuesday the Trump
administration has revoked over 300,000 US visas during his
second term.

Among visa revocations particularly condemned by rights
advocates are ⁠those of pro-Palestinian protesters demonstrating
against US ally Israel's assault on Gaza and of ‌foreigners over
social media comments about conservative commentator Charlie
Kirk's assassination.

The Trump administration's deportation attempts ​have faced
multiple legal challenges with mixed results.

news.title: Ketanji Brown Jackson Breaks With SCOTUS Voting Order as Election Looms
news.text: Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the sole dissenter in a new Supreme Court order that green-lit New Hampshire to fully ban student IDs for voting during November's midterm elections. In the order, Brown concluded, "I respectfully dissent because—even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming—I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes." New Hampshire passed a law earlier this year that said student IDs were not an acceptable form of identification to get a ballot, the Associated Press (AP) reports. What We Know The High Court's order ultimately blocks students from using their school IDs as a backup, the AP says. New Hampshire's Republican Secretary of State David Scanlan barred the IDs from being an acceptable backup after the state passed the law, the AP reports. A judge first left the law to stand as is but reversed course earlier this month, prompting the emergency appeal. The emergency appeal in Scanlan's case was ultimately granted by the High Court on Thursday. Legal Counsel for The Coalition For Open Democracy, the plaintiff in the case, called the court's order "wrong." "The Court’s decision grants a stay which both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied, blocking an injunction that has now been in place for almost three weeks, injecting confusion into the election—precisely what the Purcell principle is supposed to prevent—and authorizing an unconstitutional policy that will deprive young voters of their right to vote. "We applaud Justice Jackson for her dissent, in which she stands for the Constitution, the right to vote, and a rational application of Purcell. We will continue to vigorously litigate this case in the defense of the fundamental right to vote of young voters across New Hampshire," the statement read. The order mentions the Purcell principle, which is a legal concept in election law in the United States that advises courts against altering voting rules too close to an election. The election related ruling comes just 12 days before the midterms. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. President Donald Trump lost New Hampshire during the 2024 presidential election to then-Vice President Kamala Harris. The state's open Senate seat is rated as lean Democrat by the Cook Political Report and the governor's race is rated likely Republican by the forecaster. news.title: Indian-American Ramaswamy gets Trump’s backing on ad featuring mother of his Democratic rival Acton
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 23 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has defended Indian-American Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival Amy Acton in the Ohio governor’s race, even as Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a fellow Republican, urged that it be pulled while saying he was keeping his endorsement. “It’s wrong to run this ad,” DeWine told reporters on Thursday, according to CBS News. “I would urge Ramaswamy’s campaign to take this down.” DeWine, who is term-limited, called the ad “on its face, deeply, deeply troubling”, CBS News reported, but said he was not rescinding his endorsement of Ramaswamy. Speaking to reporters at the White House on Thursday afternoon, Trump stood by the Indian-American candidate. “All I can say is Vivek is great,” he said, according to the White House pool report. “If it’s even a little bit true, you don’t want her as governor,” Trump said. Asked why he was defending the ad when Ohio Republicans had called for it to come down, Trump said: “That’s her opinion. I’m defending it because I know that if that ad were about my mother, you would love it.” “What’s happened is the press has ganged up on a woman making a horrible statement about her daughter, and I don’t know why she should be shielded or the daughter should be shielded,” he said. “If what the mother said about the daughter is half right, she has no right even running for the governor of Ohio.” Trump also called DeWine “disloyal to the Republican Party” in a Truth Social post, ABC News reported. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries joined the attack on Ramaswamy. “Vivek Ramaswamy is a disgusting and slimy political hack,” Jeffries wrote on X on Thursday afternoon. “Every single Republican should denounce this malignant clown and rescind their support.” Vice President J.D. Vance, campaigning in Ohio on Wednesday, defended Ramaswamy for having “the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is”, according to the vice-presidential pool report. “Politics is a tough business,” Vance told reporters, according to CBS News. “And my message to my fellow elected Republicans is, if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days.” Ramaswamy campaign spokesperson Connie Luck responded to DeWine by saying “the first and only candidate to attack the mother of her opponent in this race was Amy Acton”, CBS News reported. In the ad, Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, says: “It’s not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy was a serious problem. She is a liar; she lies about her past,” according to CBS News. Acton, a former Ohio public health director, has spoken of being abused by her late stepfather, who was charged in 1978 with raping her, CBS News reported. The case never went to trial. Acton said on Thursday she had hoped Ramaswamy “wouldn’t sink this low, but of course he did”, CBS News reported. Two new polls show a tight race. A Fox News poll conducted October 15-19 had Acton at 50 per cent and Ramaswamy at 48 per cent among likely voters. A VoteHub/Verasight poll of 623 registered voters, conducted October 1-20, had Acton at 46 per cent and Ramaswamy at 45 per cent among likely voters, within the poll’s 4.2-point margin of error. VoteHub said most of its interviews were collected before the ad first aired. Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur born in Cincinnati to immigrant parents from Kerala, ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024. The election is on November 3.

news.title: Israeli fire kills four in Gaza, Syrian man
news.text:
CAIRO/JAKARTA: Israeli strikes and gunfire killed at least four people in the Gaza Strip in separate incidents on Thursday, health officials in the enclave said.

In Gaza City, a strike on a car killed at least one person, medics said. They earlier said there had been two deaths. A crowd gathered around the burning wreckage, as orange-vested emergency crews sprayed it with water, photos from the scene showed.

Other strikes killed a Palestinian man on a bike in the southern city of Khan Yunis and a man near Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, and gunfire killed a woman near the Jabalia refugee camp, in the north, the medics added.

Israel’s military said it had struck Hamas in Khan Yunis, Nuseirat and Gaza City, but that it was not aware of the reported incident in Jabalia. Israel has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks.

Francesca Albanese urges Indonesia to reconsider involvement in Trump’s Gaza board

Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal. Last year’s US-brokered ceasefire calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.

Israeli airstrikes have continued. At least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire, according to the territory’s health officials, while Israel says four soldiers have been killed.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza.

Syrian man killed

Separately, a Syrian man with a disability was killed on Thursday by Israeli fire during an incursion in the country’s south where Israel has stepped up operations.

The Israeli military has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria and conducted frequent incursions into its territory since new authorities toppled longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.

“A civilian with a disability was killed on Thursday by fire from the Israeli occupation forces during their incursion into the village of Jamla” in Daraa province, Syrian state news agency SANA reported.

Israeli forces entered a neighbourhood and placed snipers on the rooftops after bombing the area late on Wednesday, the report said.

Syria condemned “in the strongest terms the Israeli occupation forces’ crime”, a foreign ministry statement said, adding that “targeting civilians is a grave violation” of international law.

Trump’s Gaza board

Indonesia should reconsider its involvement in US President Donald Trump’s Gaza peace plan because it is being shaped by Israel and the US and lacks a Palestinian voice, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories said on Thursday.

Trump announced in January that he was setting up a “Board of Peace” to address global conflicts typically handled by the UN. Indonesia, the world’s largest Muslim-majority nation, has said it would be a member of the new body and it has also pledged troops to be deployed to Gaza as part of an international stabilisation force.

Francesca Albanese, a human rights lawyer and UN special rapporteur known for her criticism of Israel, said in an interview in Jakarta that Indonesia has historically supported the Palestinian cause but joining the board was dangerous.

Indonesia’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that its Board of Peace discussions remained on hold, reiterating its earlier position. A number of Western capitals have criticised Albanese, while the US has imposed sanctions on her.

“I understand [Indonesia’s] good intentions. I still think that it’s very dangerous, because it risks to normalise a very abnormal mechanism,” she said. Albanese said that, legally, Israel could not have a role in determining the future of Palestinians.

Rights experts have criticised Trump’s board for not including a Palestinian representative, though it is meant to supervise the temporary governance of a Palestinian territory. A board official rejected the suggestion that the Palestinians had been excluded, however, saying: “Palestinian leadership and ownership remain central to the process.” The official said Gaza’s civilian administration and recovery efforts are led by the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, which is made up of Palestinian professionals from Gaza and led by former Palestinian Authority official Ali Shaath.

news.title: Trump Says He Has ‘Right’ to Run for Third Term: ‘They Cheated Us’
news.text: President Donald Trump said Thursday that he believes he has the “right to run again” for president, despite acknowledging that the Constitution appears to bar him from seeking another term. Speaking at a campaign rally in Iowa ahead of the midterm elections, Trump raised the possibility of another presidential campaign while discussing his political standing. “I don't know who's going to be your next president,” Trump said. “And I think the law says, I'm not 100 percent sure, but I think the law says that I'm not allowed to run again.” Trump then acknowledged that he had examined the restriction and found little ambiguity. “I've studied that phrase forever,” the 80-year-old said. “Unfortunately, it's quite concise. There's not a lot of wiggle room.” But moments later, Trump suggested he nevertheless had grounds to seek the presidency again because of his continued false claim that the 2020 election was stolen from him. “They cheated us on the second one because we won it three times, so I think I have the right to run again. I think I have the right to run again because they cheated.” He continued: “They rigged the election. They rigged that.” What the Constitution Says The 22nd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution says: “No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice.” Trump was elected president in 2016 and again in 2024, meaning that another presidential election would conflict with the amendment's two-term limit. Trump has repeatedly claimed that he won the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to Joe Biden. There is no evidence that fraud altered the outcome of that election. The. Republican president enters the closing stretch of the midterm campaign with his approval rating deeply underwater. He hit record-low approval ratings of 32 percent among U.S. adults with CNN/SSRS, and 36 percent among likely voters with The New York Times/Siena University poll as the midterms enter the home stretch. Trump Has Repeatedly Teased Another Run In August, Trump told reporters that although he would like to run again, the constitutional restriction appeared firm. “I’d love to run, but the law is very strong,” Trump said. “Everybody wants me to do it, but the law is very strong.” The comments followed months of Trump publicly entertaining another campaign. During the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner in July, he donned a red “Trump 2028” hat and told the audience: “I won three times. Now, I’m going to do it again.” Trump has also shared “Trump 2028” imagery on social media, while his allies have periodically discussed potential ways he could remain in power beyond the end of his current term. At other moments, however, Trump has spoken about leaving the White House in January 2029 and watching his successor from home. His latest remarks in Iowa went further by offering a specific justification for why he believes he should be permitted to run again. news.title: Charley Hull Reveals Truth Behind Viral Guilty Pleasure Photo
news.text:
Charley Hull answers questions with a quiet confidence that is difficult to miss. It is the kind of composure associated with someone who knows exactly who she is—and what she can achieve.

Self-assured is perhaps the most fitting description of the British golfer, who is ranked eighth in the Rolex Women’s World Golf Rankings. Hull is also determined to remain authentic, speaking candidly about her opinions and parts of her personal life that many professional athletes prefer to keep private.

Her social media accounts offer the clearest glimpse of that openness. Images of a glamorous lifestyle appear alongside tournament trophies and clips from her fitness sessions. Even the Instagram bio of the 30-year-old, whose account has more than 860,000 followers, reflects her direct approach: “Shy kids don’t get sweets.”

Hull’s growing fame in recent years has been driven in part by that unfiltered online presence, particularly after a photograph of her walking the golf course with a cigarette in her mouth went viral. Against that backdrop, her appearance at the on!vitational felt fitting—a nicotine-sponsored celebrity simulator golf tournament held at the SoFi Center in South Florida.

Hull will return to the state-of-the-art venue regularly in the weeks ahead for the inaugural season of the WTGL. The women’s counterpart to the TGL simulator league will feature Hull alongside Lydia Ko, Rose Zhang, Michelle Wie and Lexi Thompson, among others.

Before taking her first swings in the simulator, Hull spoke exclusively with Our News Outlet about the new competition, her public image and the future of women’s sport.

She has only a few minutes to talk, pausing between bites of food—despite her frustration that her order is wrong—and brief conversations with her fellow Team Malbon competitors.

Although Hull expects to spend several weeks at the Florida indoor golf facility once the WTGL begins in November, she intends to return to the UK whenever possible.

“I literally fly home and fly back,” Hull told Our News Outlet, underlining how strongly she feels about her family and hometown. “I’ve been in America before for a couple days photo shoot. I flew home for 24 hours, then just to come back to America and do the same spot because I miss home that much.”

“You know what I like?” she added. “I just like waking up in my own area, my own bed, knowing that I can go see my mum and my dad, go and see my friends, just do normal things. And I like being around mum and my dad a lot. I have great parents. I couldn’t have asked for a better mum and dad growing up.”

Hull was recently back in Britain, where she shared a series of photographs from a celebration for her friend and fellow professional golfer Georgia Hall.

“She had a baby and it’s her wedding in a few months’ time, so I took her away,” Hull said, explaining that the pair spent time at Estelle Manor.

The photograph that attracted the most attention showed Hull in a light blue bikini, highlighting her toned stomach and legs. The post, which collected more than 50,000 likes, also included images of her in dressing gowns and cocktail outfits.

“That was so much fun. We were having mini photo shoots in the room. I thought it was a nice bikini picture, so that’s why I posted it. I’m proud of my body.”

Hull’s confidence was underscored again on Thursday, when she told fans that she had taken part in a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit photo shoot—one of her most revealing public appearances to date.

With the caption “I did a thing…,” Hull posed wearing only a towel, prompting an immediate surge of reaction in the comments on Instagram. The date for the full photo shoot’s release has not yet been confirmed.

On her recent girls’ trip, meanwhile, Hull reveals that she decided to take all her photos on a Canon camera, instead of her phone: ‘I wanted to get that because I thought I want to capture these moments without being on my phone there.’

With her rise to fame within the world of golf and beyond, Hull’s time is more precious than ever: ‘I haven’t got as much time as I’d like to, so I’m looking forward to this offseason just to completely get away and just chill with my friends and family at home.’

The choice to show off as much of her life as she does differs from the norm. Hull’s penchant for posting what some may call behind the scenes content stems less from a naivety but more of how she views herself.

‘I don’t see myself as somebody famous,’ she admitted. ‘I just see myself as just a good golfer, and I just post like my friends post who don’t play golf, who aren’t in the public eye. Yeah, that’s just the way I am.’

DON’T MISS: Is Stray Kids Felix Bi? Sexuality And Partner 2024

In truth, though, her fame has skyrocketed in recent months, and she can even count the president among her biggest fans.

Hull was invited to join Donald Trump for a state banquet at Windsor Castle last month, and she later revealed he had even asked her for a round of golf. 

‘I spoke to him last night and he has invited me (to play),’ Hull told BBC Radio 5 Live at the time.

‘He has said he wants to sort a game out. That is pretty cool. Last year he reached out actually to my agent and he wanted to play at the end of the year but I think I was going on holiday.

‘We spoke about it last night and we are really going to try and sort a game out before the end of the year, which will be pretty cool.’

The on!vitational marked Hull’s first time hitting on the simulator. While Malbon ended up falling to eventual winners Team Grass League, featuring the likes of Paige Spiranac, Hull will aim to have more success with Atlanta Drive GC in WTGL. Hull is joined by Minjee Lee, Andrea Lee, Yuka Saso and Nataliya Guseva as one of five teams in the league.

There are plans and hopes to expand past the inaugural season, much like their men’s league counterparts. But that’s not the only parallel between the two leagues. Much like how men’s world No 1 Scottie Scheffler is not on a TGL team, women’s world No 1 Nelly Korda is also absent from the WTGL roster.

But Korda’s reasons are specific. In January, she called it a ‘huge and unbelievable miss’ for the stars of the LPGA to compete alongside and against the men in TGL.

‘It would have been the first time that men and women were on the same playing field,’ she told Golfweek at the time. ‘But I also think it’s great that we are getting this opportunity, so those are my mixed feelings.’

TGL co-founder Rory McIlroy disagreed with Korda’s assessment, saying: ‘I think when we talked about WTGL, obviously there were talks of a mixed team… But I do think that it is important to give the women their own platform and encourage them to grow that themselves.’

Hull agrees with McIlroy: ‘I can understand [Nelly], where she’s coming from. But, I do think it’s a great opportunity. You’ve got to start somewhere and the men play here, so now they’ve started the WTGL for us, which is great. But who’s to say that they won’t probably pursue something in the future of us playing together?’

It’s an interesting time to start a women’s professional sports league in the United States. While women’s sports are perhaps more popular than they ever have been, they also have become a lightning rod for controversy – especially the WNBA.

Much of that controversy is less about the players themselves and more about the perception of women athletes from outsiders. Many comments and debates on social media revolve around the shock of some people to find that women are, in fact, very competitive when it comes to professional sports.

Other debates center around the way female athletes look and present themselves compared with their male counterparts.

When asking Hull about these discussions, she took a pause before offering her thoughts: ‘I think that women have got an advantage in sports for a whole different audience to what men in sports have. 

‘So rather than sexualize it and look down on it and say you’re turning sports backwards, embrace it and also be good at the sport. Like, so what if a pretty girl is playing good? She’s pretty, she looks good and she’s playing good. 

‘And then so what if there’s someone else who just loves playing their sport and doesn’t care what they look like, and they’re playing good as well? No one should be frowned upon. I think you should just embrace all of it.’

Later, she added: ‘I think, naturally, if you were to put me against a 30-year-old male that has been playing golf the same time as me, they are naturally stronger. If there’s 100 men and there’s 100 women, the percentage of the men being better than the women are not necessarily more skillful, it’s because they’re more powerful.

‘But then you’ll get a couple women that will beat them, even the top ones. And I think that’s something that’s really cool. I don’t think it should be “the man’s better than the women or the women’s better than the men.” It’s an achievement to get to the top of your sport whether you’re a man or a woman.’ 

As for the other debate, where men may be shocked to discover how competitive women athletes are, Hull cracked a wry smile when asked if she finds it patronizing.

‘No, I love it,’ she said with a grin. ‘Because it bites them in the butt. I love it because then it’s just like “ha!” you know what I mean? Like it kind of makes me want to strive to do better.’

news.title: Trump’s Tacky Arch Project Hit With New Setback
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s quest to build a 250-foot-tall “triumphal arch” has hit its latest roadblock as he tries to speed the project toward construction.

The president’s lawyers laid out an eye-popping timeline in court filings Wednesday, revealing that Trump is hoping to secure permission for the gargantuan monument and begin work as early as Nov. 5.

But three veterans and a retired architectural historian suing the Trump administration to stop construction of the tacky arch moved to slam the brakes on the project on Thursday, asking District Judge Tanya Chutkan to prohibit the administration and the National Park Service “from taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction of, any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization, during the pendency of this litigation,” according to the Associated Press. 

The National Planning Commission is scheduled to consider the final approval of the site and building plans on Nov. 5—two days after the midterms—potentially clearing the way for work to start that day if the Trump-controlled Interior Department also approves.

“NPS may publish such notice as early as November 5, 2026, and construction could commence as early as November 5, 2026,” the president’s notice said Wednesday. 

In Thursday’s filing, the plaintiffs argued that the notice “makes clear that the defendants have no intention of awaiting this court’s decision on the cross-motions for summary judgment and have every intention of imminently beginning construction of the arch on Memorial Circle.”

Chutkan, an Obama appointee, has now given the two sides until noon Friday to hash out a briefing schedule and file it with the court.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 

Trump’s latest architectural monstrosity, which is estimated to cost at least $100 million, would tower over Memorial Circle, opposite Arlington National Cemetery.

The plaintiffs in the lawsuit are arguing that the arch needs to be approved by Congress, and say it would degrade the cemetery and ruin historic views across the nation’s capital. 

The arch is the subject of another lawsuit brought by the Arlington County Board in Virginia, which is accusing federal agencies of ignoring environmental and safety standards in the rush to build the so-called “Arc de Trump.”

Trump has previously claimed that the extravagant arch could serve a second purpose as a military stronghold, stocked with drones, sniper positions, and ammunition, though blueprints published last week describe it simply as a “ceremonial gateway.”

Americans opposed the arch by more than 2-to-1, with 52 percent opposed, 21 percent in favor, and 26 percent unsure, in an April Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos survey. Strong opposition (41 percent) outweighed strong support (9 percent) by over 4-to-1.

news.title: US accuses Canada of election meddling
news.text:
The US has accused Canadian officials of attempting to interfere in American elections, citing politically targeted trade measures, anti-Trump advertising campaigns and meetings with Democratic politicians ahead of next month’s midterms.

In a fact sheet published on Wednesday, the US Embassy in Ottawa accused Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government of openly seeking to influence American politics.

“The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in US elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances,” the embassy stated.

The document singled out Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly, citing her remarks about deliberately targeting Republican-leaning states with retaliatory tariffs in response to President Donald Trump’s trade policies.

“We’re making sure to put pressure on American businesses, in key Republican states to put pressure on the Trump Administration,” Joly said in March. “We’re being wise and strategic to put political pressure,” she added in August.

Washington also questioned Joly’s meetings with Democratic officials in Boston and Chicago in September, as well as an anti-tariff advertising campaign launched by Ontario Premier Doug Ford featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticizing protectionist trade policies.

The embassy also highlighted a recent appearance by Canadian Consul General Bernadette Jordan alongside two Democratic congressmen at a Vermont roundtable on trade tensions, just three weeks before the midterms. It also cited a Canadian government billboard campaign targeting 12 mostly Republican-voting states and Washington, DC.

The embassy also cited Liberal lawmaker Anthony Housefather’s campaigning for Democratic Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz in Florida, and listed 11 Canadians who had been charged or sentenced in 2026 for illegally voting in previous American elections.

“All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence US elections in any way,” the statement concluded. “Americans decide America’s elections.”

The accusations followed a warning from US Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, who said Washington was closely watching Canadian political activities ahead of the November 3 congressional elections.

“We’re monitoring it, we’re evaluating it and if some of it becomes election interference then America will respond to it,” Hoekstra said.

Ottawa has rejected the allegations. Carney insisted that Canada’s measures were intended to protect its workers and businesses from American tariffs, while Ford denied any interest in meddling in US elections. Joly defended her meetings with American politicians as normal diplomacy, pointing out that she had engaged with both Republicans and Democrats.

The dispute comes amid deteriorating relations between the neighboring countries, driven by Trump’s sweeping tariffs and repeated suggestions that Canada should become America’s 51st state.

In September, Carney revealed that his government had examined the possibility of US military action against Canada, describing the scenario as an “extreme tail risk” that nevertheless warranted contingency planning. Ottawa, meanwhile, has been seeking closer military and economic ties with Europe to reduce its dependence on Washington.
news.summary:
Washington has warned Ottawa against attempts to influence the upcoming midterms, citing anti-Trump advertising and meetings with Democrats

news.title: Trump administration stopped sharing evidence in Good and Pretti killings, Minnesota officials say
news.text:
The federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers, state officials said in recent court filings.

Minnesota officials sued President Donald Trump's administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings during Trump’s immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year. The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don’t have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don’t trust the federal government to investigate itself.

The state is still seeking the cell phones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews.

State prosecutors announced in July that the federal government had begun turning over evidence in the cases, including police body camera video and hard drives containing statements. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said at the time that the state expected to receive “all the evidence.”

But Minnesota investigators said in October court filings that the transfer of evidence stopped soon after the July announcement. Moriarty said the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Minnesota told her on Sept. 10 that evidence sharing would be on pause indefinitely “in light of challenges with D.C.," according to the documents. 

State prosecutors have again asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing they "have identified no legal authority or rational basis justifying their obstruction of state criminal investigations."

In a reply filed Tuesday, attorneys for the Justice Department argued it's within their discretion to decline to share information with state authorities. They cited the department's rules for responding to record requests, known as the Touhy regulations, which apply only when formal legal proceedings are underway. The attorneys said there was no active court case when Minnesota made its requests.

Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, said in a legal declaration that federal authorities still have Good’s clothing, the cell phone of the officer who killed her and interview recordings that state authorities have never been able to view.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer fatally shot Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, while she was leaving a Minneapolis protest on Jan. 7. Bystander video shows Good in the driver’s seat of an SUV, repeatedly honking the horn, when masked immigration officers order her to step out of the vehicle. She starts to pull forward, and an officer standing in front of the car fires at her windshield. The officer, now standing about an arm’s length from the open window on the driver's side, fires twice more, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense.

Good's death and that of Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse who was killed weeks later by a federal officer in Minneapolis, ignited nationwide protests against the Republican president's immigration enforcement efforts. 

No criminal charges have been filed in connection with the fatal shootings.

Evans said the federal government also has not shared a recorded statement from an officer who shot Pretti, the firearms used by the officers, their phones, projectiles and casings, and a gun taken from Pretti before he was shot.
news.summary: State officials say in court filings that the federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers

news.title: New York City bans horse-drawn carriages from 2028
news.text:
The New York City Council has voted to ban horse-drawn carriages from city streets and Central Park, ending a historic tourist attraction and longstanding industry.

Forty of the city's 51 council members supported the bill, which was backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who earlier this month said the horse-drawn carriage industry would come to an end. 

Seven voted against it and two abstained.

If the mayor signs it, the ban will go into effect in June of 2028.

The lead-up is meant to help the approximately 150 active carriage drivers find new employment, city council speaker Julie Menin said.

Critics say the animals suffer, pointing to deadly collapses and dangerous escapes, while advocates point to the jobs they create and the heritage they uphold.

The bill included a provision for exploring potential compensation for licence holders, Ms Menin said.

It prevents owners of the nearly 200 horses from selling them for slaughter or for other horse-carriage businesses.

Support for the ban grew after the death this summer of Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old tourist from India. 

Mr Mahajan was thrown from a carriage and died on June 17, when the horse ​bolted after the driver stepped away to take a picture of Mahajan's family.

That followed a series of other incidents with the carriages, including the deaths of several horses.

The Central Park Conservancy, which manages the US's most frequented urban park with 42 million annual visits, threw its weight behind the calls for a ban, saying it had become "a matter of public health and safety".

US President Donald Trump, who has both attacked Mamdani and held cordial meetings with him, expressed scepticism about the ban.

"When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don't stop cars from entering the Park," Mr Trump wrote.

Mr Trump's business empire is headquartered in Trump Tower, minutes from Central Park.

The day before the vote, the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage business owners and drivers, said that if the bill was enacted, it would seek a temporary restraining order from a court "the minute the ink dries", according to a letter sent to New York City Corporation counsel Steve Banks.

"This may be the first time in City history that a previously licensed profession was banned," the letter signed by principal attorney Arthur Schwartz said. 

"The proposed bill deprives the owner of all economically beneficial or productive use of their property."

news.summary: The New York City Council votes to ban horse-drawn carriages from city streets and Central Park.

news.title: Karoline Leavitt speaks out on 'tough' Katie Zacharia exit as press secretary
news.text: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has broken her silence after her ex-boss, US President Donald Trump , axed her replacement less than a week into the role. Mr Trump dismissed his new press secretary Katie Zacharia on Friday, 16 October. She was brought in on Monday, 12 October , but encountered a backlash after just one briefing and growing doubts about her credentials. The episode has left Mr Trump without a public spokesperson weeks ahead of November's midterm elections. Ms Leavitt has revealed that she's offered to assist US President Donald Trump in selecting "someone who can serve him and the country well". Chatting with FOX News Digital's Paul Steinhauser, Ms Leavitt remarked, "Well, look, White House Press Secretary is a tough job. "I know that because I did it, obviously, for almost two years. And many people say it's one of the hardest jobs in politics ." She explained the position "takes a lot of preparation" and "sometimes you don't know how someone will perform until they go out there." Ms Leavitt extended her best wishes to her successor. "So, look, as the president said, we wish Katie the best. The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well," she stated. "And I think - I know the President is continuing to look over options." Ms Leavitt noted the position is highly coveted and that she needed to "help to the President to help him select someone who can serve him and the country well." When asked what advice she would offer the US leader should he request it, Ms Leavitt was guarded. "Well, I'll keep my private counsel to the President private," she said. "But I do obviously talk to him about what the job entails, and he knows it very well," she added. "Nobody understands the press better than Donald Trump." According to Leavitt, the president requires someone who "is tough, who is smart, who understands his policies, who is loyal, and who can go out there and put up a fight. "There's a lot of qualified people who can have it," Leavitt continued. "It's just up to the president to make that decision." Mr Trump revealed last week that he had urged Ms Zacharia to "reconsider" her position within his administration. He maintained the choice was hers, yet the tone of official statements hinted at Ms Zacharia having been let go. "Katie's been treated very badly by the media. Very, very badly. Very unfairly, I think. And I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" he told reporters. "Because, you know, she's been treated very rough," he added. "And she's a nice person. Very nice person. I've watched her on television for years. But I said, 'Is this for you, Katie?'". "You don't need this. You don't have to be treated. I would say the fake news, but just generally, the media has been very rough." Commenting on her appearance on Sean Hannity on Thursday, Mr Trump, who caught the interview on Friday morning, remarked: "She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily." Mr Trump also told Ms Zacharia, "You don't have to do this if you don't want to. "I said to her, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider'," he said. "She's got a beautiful husband and family. I met the family yesterday. Beautiful kids. It's like a picture postcard." The White House, when approached by The Mirror US for comment, directed attention to a tweet stating, "A senior White House official tells @pdoocy Katie ZACHARIA is 'transitioning out' of the press secretary position." Ms Zacharia confirmed her exit from the White House in a post on X. "President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man," she wrote. "I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to," she added. "It was an honour to work for him."
news.summary: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has spoken out after her successor Katie Zacharia departed the role less than one week after being appointed by US President Donald Trump

news.title: ‘Starshield Still Limited’ – Zelensky Says Ukraine Cannot Fully Intercept Russian Drones Despite Restoration Claims
news.text:
Ukraine’s military satellite communications remain restricted, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour published Thursday, Oct. 22, warning that the limitations continue to undermine Ukraine’s ability to intercept fast-moving Russian attack drones.

Separately, US President Donald Trump said Thursday that Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s satellite service, but declined to confirm whether he personally intervened to have the restrictions lifted.

“I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters, responding to a Wall Street Journal report that he had called Musk and requested the restoration of the service.

In the CNN interview, Zelensky described continuing restrictions on Starlink and Starshield, SpaceX’s satellite communications services used by Ukrainian forces.

“Now it’s still limited,” Zelensky said.

He explained that Ukraine had developed high-speed interceptor drones capable of destroying Russian jet-powered Shaheds, but the restrictions had severely reduced their operational capabilities.

“When an Iranian drone goes with a speed of 450 or 500 kilometers per hour, and you limit [the speed] one night to 70 or even 100, you cannot intercept anything,” Zelensky said.

“And this is terrible.”

It was not immediately clear whether Zelensky’s interview was recorded before or after Trump’s announcement that the service had been restored.

‘It means limiting our ability to defend ourselves’

Zelensky said Ukraine had developed an effective new method of intercepting Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which can reach speeds of 400–500 kilometers per hour.

The interceptors rely on satellite communications that remain connected while drones travel at high speeds.

But Ukrainian forces experienced sudden restrictions that sharply reduced the maximum speed at which the equipment could maintain connectivity.

The Ukrainian president said the limitations appeared overnight, disrupting operations that had become essential to protecting Ukrainian cities.

Some restrictions were subsequently eased, allowing equipment to operate at somewhat higher speeds, but the original capabilities had not been fully restored.

Zelensky stressed that the consequences were particularly serious because the restrictions affected defensive operations inside Ukraine.

“That’s why it was strange they limited us in Ukraine,” he said.

“It means limiting our ability to defend ourselves.”

The president pointed out that Russia’s newer jet-powered Shaheds were being deployed against Ukrainian schools, universities, bridges, energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure.

Ukrainian officials have previously reported that satellite connections were being lost at speeds around 160 kilometers per hour, far below the requirements for some high-speed drone interceptors.

Asked who ordered Starshield restrictions, Zelensky says he does not know

Asked who was responsible for limiting Ukraine’s satellite communications, Zelensky said he did not know whether the decision originated with SpaceX or government institutions.

“I don’t know,” he said.

“Technically, I think SpaceX can do it. But whether the decision comes from them or from some institutions, I don’t know.”

The question of responsibility has become increasingly contentious in Washington.

Musk has said Starshield, the military-grade satellite service, is controlled by the US government, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio has maintained that Starlink is a commercial product whose operating decisions are made by SpaceX.

Rubio has also said that Ukraine’s request for broader access to Starshield remains under discussion.

The Pentagon has denied issuing instructions to slow the system.

The conflicting accounts have left the cause of the restrictions unresolved, even as Ukrainian forces continue to report reduced capabilities.

Zelensky: Ukraine does not use Starlink for strikes inside Russia

Zelensky underscored that Ukraine does not use Starlink to strike Russian military or energy facilities inside Russia, drawing a distinction between those operations and the satellite communications needed to defend Ukrainian cities.

“We don’t attack Russian military targets or energy targets using Starlink. Never,” he said.

The president explained that Ukraine had previously requested additional satellite-supported capabilities to target Russian ballistic missile launchers, which threaten Ukrainian civilians.

He argued that destroying those launchers could prevent further missile attacks, particularly when Ukraine lacks sufficient Patriot interceptors.

However, Washington had not granted the requested access.

“The Americans never gave us this,” Zelensky said.

He emphasized that the current restrictions were affecting Ukraine’s defensive operations on its own territory rather than limiting strikes inside Russia.

US ballistic missile warning intelligence restored after talks with Rubio

Zelensky also confirmed that Ukraine’s access to critical early-warning intelligence about Russian ballistic missile launches had been restored following discussions with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

He said Ukraine had experienced serious problems receiving warnings, leaving civilians without crucial information needed to reach shelters before incoming missiles struck.

“We had real problems with intelligence,” Zelensky said.

He explained that the missing information concerned Russian ballistic missile launches and was essential to protecting the civilian population.

“We didn’t get this message. That’s why it was so dangerous for us.”

Zelensky said he raised the matter directly with Rubio and requested the restoration of intelligence sharing.

“Now intelligence works,” he confirmed.

“Thanks to the secretary, thanks to Congress, thanks to the president. I don’t know who did it, but thanks. It came back.”

Rubio has denied that the US ordered any interruption in intelligence sharing, saying American policy had not changed.

‘If you give something to Putin, he will want everything’

Zelensky also strongly opposed easing sanctions against Russia, warning that additional revenues would allow Moscow to finance its continuing invasion.

His remarks followed disagreements over recent US decisions affecting Russian energy exports.

The Ukrainian president emphasized that his concerns were not personal disagreements with Trump but reflected Ukraine’s security interests.

“I think that if you lift sanctions, you make him stronger,” Zelensky said.

He warned that concessions would not satisfy the Kremlin.

“If you give something to Putin, he will need everything. He will want everything, and will not calm down before he has it all.”

Zelensky argued that increasing Russian revenues would provide additional resources for Moscow’s military campaign.

“And it will only give much more money for Putin for this war. And that’s why I’m against it.”

He stressed that Ukraine’s position was not simply about the amount of land under Russian control.

“For us, our land is very important. Because it’s about people. It’s not about kilometers,” he said.

Zelensky noted that Ukrainians had sacrificed their lives defending the country’s sovereignty and independence.

“Nobody will recognize these territories which are temporarily occupied as Russian territories,” he said.

He said Ukraine was prepared to pursue negotiations aimed at stopping the killing, regardless of the terminology used.

“We can call it ceasefire. We can call it stop the killings. We can call it freeze the conflict,” he said.

“The only one thing what is important – not the name, the result.”

Zelensky insisted that any discussion concerning Ukrainian territory must involve Ukraine directly and take place at the level of national leaders.

“Putin is playing, you know. He’s a player,” Zelensky said.

“It’s a pity because he plays with the lives of other people.”

Despite the continuing Russian attacks, Zelensky described his recent meeting with US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Oslo as productive.

He expressed hope that further negotiations could produce progress toward ending the war.

He warned that Moscow’s objective remained to destroy Ukraine’s infrastructure, undermine civilian morale and weaken the country’s ability to defend itself.

‘Don’t forget about us’ – Zelensky appeals for Patriots and full satellite access

Zelensky closed the interview with an appeal for additional Patriot interceptor missiles and the restoration of satellite communications needed to defend Ukrainian cities.

Acknowledging Washington’s focus on the Middle East, he stressed that Ukraine was not asking the US to abandon its other commitments.

“We don’t want to compare. We’re just asking not to forget about us,” Zelensky said.

Ukraine was prepared to pay for additional interceptors, he emphasized, but European-funded supplies remained insufficient to protect the country from Russian attacks.

Despite the shortages and continuing restrictions, Zelensky vowed that Ukraine would keep fighting, regardless of whether its partners could immediately meet its requests.

“We will do everything to bring peace closer, but we will not let Putin win this war.”

He confirms US missile-warning intelligence has resumed, urges more Patriot interceptors and opposes easing sanctions on Moscow.

news.title: Russia, Ukraine trade attacks after US envoy meets Putin
news.text:
Witkoff briefs Russian president on ‘new aspects in approaches of Europeans and Kyiv’ from Oslo meeting
• Moscow mayor says 630 drones launched towards region
• Russian strikes injure 15 people in Kyiv
• Kremlin aide tells media Russia ready to resume trilateral talks in mid-November

KYIV: Russia and Ukraine traded major attacks overnight, with Moscow’s mayor saying on Thursday that 630 drones had been launched towards the region, shortly after a US envoy held talks with the Russian president in Saint Petersburg.

It was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war, US President Donald Trump said after his envoy Steve Witkoff’s meeting with Vladimir Putin on Wednesday.

The Kremlin indicated it was “in principle” open to the resumption of trilateral talks between the two sides with the United States.

But attacks did not let up in the wake of the visit, with Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko posting on social media that strikes had wounded 15 people in the Ukrainian capital, eight of whom needed hospitalisation.

He said in a separate post that strikes had damaged metro infrastructure at the Pivdenny Bridge, which officials said had restricted traffic between parts of the city.

Ukraine’s airforce posted a war-ning in the early hours of “more ballistic missiles towards Kyiv” and ins-tructed residents to stay in shelters.

Moscow’s mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that two people had been wounded during mostly-intercepted barrages of 630 drones headed towards the region, 163 of which were approaching the capital city.

Witkoff had flown to Russia from a meeting with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, which was aimed at smoothing over a bitter rift between Trump and the Ukrainian leader.

Witkoff praised Putin as a “humanitarian” for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard, but the Kremlin warned after the meeting that while Moscow was “in principle” willing to restart talks there was little “substance” in Ukrainian and European peace proposals the US diplomat had delivered.

Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Russia was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral talks in mid-November — after the US midterm elections — and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on post-war security.

‘Work left to do’

Ushakov said Witkoff brie-fed Putin on “some new asp-ects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv” from the Oslo meeting, adding though that “there wasn’t really much substance in them”.

A summit between Putin, Trump and China’s Xi Jinping was also being prepared in China’s Shenzhen for next month, Ushakov said, calling it “the first such meeting in history”.

During their three-hour meeting, Witkoff praised Putin for granting Trump’s request to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a “mercenary” fighting for Ukraine.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian — you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said.

news.title: Trump Signs Order Targeting Costs of Single-Family Housing
news.text:
President Donald Trump took aim at lowering housing costs across the country Oct. 22 by ordering his administration to create a pilot program to cancel mortgage insurance, lower closing costs and mortgage rates for some borrowers, and boost manufactured homes.

“The American Dream of homeownership is a vital pillar of our great country,” Trump said in the executive order. “It is the policy of my Administration to reduce regulatory barriers to mortgage origination and costs impeding homeownership.”

The president also said he wanted to incorporate technology and artificial intelligence to lower costs and promote competition and innovation in the housing and mortgage markets.

The order directs Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency Bill Pulte, who oversees the federal Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the 11 federal home loan banks, to create a test program to automatically cancel private mortgage insurance payments for certain qualifying homeowners once they have built up enough equity in their homes.

This is expected to save some homeowners from paying the high costs for insurance every month, the White House said. Only mortgages obtained after the program starts will qualify.

Pulte said in a post on X that the initiative was “the greatest Housing Executive Order in History.”

Pulte, who also serves as the chairman of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, said the actions in the order would help Americans save thousands of dollars.

Pulte and Department of Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner will co-chair the Task Force on Manufactured Housing Innovation.

The committee is tasked with increasing the quality of manufactured housing and streamlining the permitting and regulatory burdens associated with building them.

The order also directed the task force to lower the cost of home building by making it easier to use modern manufacturing methods in factory-built housing production, among other actions.

“President Trump is a builder, and today he is committing to bring even more innovation and affordable housing solutions to market for the American People,” Turner said. “The Task Force on Manufactured Housing Innovation will continue to slash red tape, unleash private sector innovation, and deliver housing affordability for American families.”

The order also calls for Pulte to find ways to reduce excessive title insurance, especially in refinancing.

The federal Agriculture and Veterans Affairs secretaries are also ordered to reduce the interest rates charged on single-family home loans made directly by their departments.

The National Association of Realtors applauded Trump’s initiative to lower housing costs and “continued efforts to make housing more affordable and expand access to the American dream of homeownership.”

“President Trump’s latest Executive Order helps address the costs associated with homeownership and takes steps toward making homeownership more sustainable for American families,” Shannon McGahn, executive vice president and chief advocacy officer of the association, said in a statement.

The administration’s efforts come at a time when the U.S. housing supply continues to increase.

Existing home sales increased by 1.5 percent month over month in September, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Although sales have increased month to month in the south and west, year-over-year sales have declined nationwide. The higher inventory and longer days on the market give buyers better negotiating power, the association’s chief economist, Lawrence Yun, said.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury also issued proposed regulations Thursday to make homeownership more affordable.

The ROAD to Housing Act would restrict large institutional investors from buying single-family homes. It would also codify Trump’s executive order, signed in January, restricting the purchase of single-family homes by investors, integrating it into permanent regulations.

Starting on Jan. 7, 2027, large institutional investors may not purchase or enter into a contract to buy single-family homes unless it qualifies as an exception. The investors are defined as businesses that invest in, own, rent, manage, or control at least 350 homes.

The rule has to go through a process before it is adopted. The public has 30 days to comment on it.
news.summary: The order is expected to bring innovation to the housing industry and lower costs by thousands for some homeowners.

news.title: Indian-American Ramaswamy gets Trump’s backing on ad featuring mother of his Democratic rival Acton
news.text:
Washington, Oct 23 (SocialNews.XYZ) US President Donald Trump has defended Indian-American Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival Amy Acton in the Ohio governor’s race, even as Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a fellow Republican, urged that it be pulled while saying he was keeping his endorsement.

“It’s wrong to run this ad,” DeWine told reporters on Thursday, according to CBS News. “I would urge Ramaswamy’s campaign to take this down.”

DeWine, who is term-limited, called the ad “on its face, deeply, deeply troubling”, CBS News reported, but said he was not rescinding his endorsement of Ramaswamy.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Thursday afternoon, Trump stood by the Indian-American candidate. “All I can say is Vivek is great,” he said, according to the White House pool report.

“If it’s even a little bit true, you don’t want her as governor,” Trump said.

Asked why he was defending the ad when Ohio Republicans had called for it to come down, Trump said: “That’s her opinion. I’m defending it because I know that if that ad were about my mother, you would love it.”

“What’s happened is the press has ganged up on a woman making a horrible statement about her daughter, and I don’t know why she should be shielded or the daughter should be shielded,” he said. “If what the mother said about the daughter is half right, she has no right even running for the governor of Ohio.”

Trump also called DeWine “disloyal to the Republican Party” in a Truth Social post, ABC News reported.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries joined the attack on Ramaswamy. “Vivek Ramaswamy is a disgusting and slimy political hack,” Jeffries wrote on X on Thursday afternoon. “Every single Republican should denounce this malignant clown and rescind their support.”

Vice President J.D. Vance, campaigning in Ohio on Wednesday, defended Ramaswamy for having “the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is”, according to the vice-presidential pool report.

“Politics is a tough business,” Vance told reporters, according to CBS News. “And my message to my fellow elected Republicans is, if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days.”

Ramaswamy campaign spokesperson Connie Luck responded to DeWine by saying “the first and only candidate to attack the mother of her opponent in this race was Amy Acton”, CBS News reported.

In the ad, Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, says: “It’s not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy was a serious problem. She is a liar; she lies about her past,” according to CBS News. Acton, a former Ohio public health director, has spoken of being abused by her late stepfather, who was charged in 1978 with raping her, CBS News reported. The case never went to trial.

Acton said on Thursday she had hoped Ramaswamy “wouldn’t sink this low, but of course he did”, CBS News reported.

Two new polls show a tight race. A Fox News poll conducted October 15-19 had Acton at 50 per cent and Ramaswamy at 48 per cent among likely voters.

A VoteHub/Verasight poll of 623 registered voters, conducted October 1-20, had Acton at 46 per cent and Ramaswamy at 45 per cent among likely voters, within the poll’s 4.2-point margin of error. VoteHub said most of its interviews were collected before the ad first aired.

Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur born in Cincinnati to immigrant parents from Kerala, ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024. The election is on November 3.

news.title: 76ers come from 29 down to beat Cavs in home opener
news.text:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Tyrese Maxey scored 32 points and Joel Embiid had 24 to help LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers wipe out a 29-point deficit in their home opener and stun the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106 on Thursday night.

James had 17 points and 10 rebounds in the biggest comeback win of his career, and fellow newcomer Jaylen Brown had 21 points in game that already may be tough for the Sixers to top this season, which they’ve started with wins over the NBA champion Knicks and the Eastern Conference finalist Cavaliers.

The Sixers refused to go down without a fight and nearly got into one when Maxey and his former Philadelphia teammate James Harden went nose-to-nose in the fourth before they were separated. Maxey was relentless on defense and was the catalyst for a 15-0 run in the fourth that gave the Sixers the lead and left the Cavaliers fumbling for answers.

Donovan Mitchell scored 32 points for the Cavs in their season opener.

James flirted in free agency with a third stint in Cleveland before he signed a two-year deal with the Sixers for the veteran minimum.

He won one of his four NBA titles with the Cavaliers and is trying to add a fifth ring in Philadelphia. The hype for the home opener was real, with tickets listed on secondary markets for around $4,000 in the lower bowl. The win against the Knicks only cranked up the enthusiasm for the first look in Philly at James and Brown — and they responded with an opener to remember.

The 41-year-old James — accused Thursday by President Donald Trump of disrespecting the United States by not standing still during the national anthem — had his moments. He brought the crowd to life with an uncontested two-handed jam in the first half and later a bucket off a steal by Maxey.

The Sixers missed 11 of 15 3-pointers and had 14 turnovers (only 12 total against the Knicks) in the first half and the packed house erupted in boos late in the second period.

Mitchell scored 22 points in the half as the Cavaliers stretched their lead to 29 points. That advantage was gone when Embiid scored seven straight points in the fourth to make it 96-95.

No matter the outcome, fans of both teams who watched on TV had something to complain about. A new lighting system at the 76ers’ arena appeared to bathe the court in a blue hue and added heavy colorized streaks and reflections from cameras on the ESPN broadcast.

Cavaliers: Have their home opener Saturday against Brooklyn.

76ers: Play back-to-back games at home this weekend — Saturday against Milwaukee and Sunday against Detroit.
