news.title: This Is the Sordid Reason Trump Bows to Putin: Author
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s overtures to Russian dictator Vladimir Putin may reflect his hopes for life after the presidency, his biographer says. 

Trump, 80, has delivered a string of wins for Putin, 74, this month while his relationship with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has reached one of its lowest points since he returned to office, drawing him closer to Moscow while pushing America further apart from its traditional European allies. 

Trump on Friday struck a deal with Putin to lift congressionally approved sanctions against Russian oil companies, after allowing Russia to export diesel to the U.S. 

Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces faced sustained restrictions on their use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network that has become a critical tool in Ukraine’s defenses against Russian attacks. Several administration insiders told The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday that Trump had full knowledge of the reduction in Starshield service, though Trump has denied the claims.

“Who among us thought that we would see an American president side with the aggressor, side with Russia?” co-host Joanna Coles said during a live taping of the Inside Trump’s Head podcast at the Teragram Ballroom in Los Angeles on Tuesday. 

Co-host Michael Wolff noted that Trump’s enduring coziness with Putin has fueled speculation throughout both of his presidencies that the Russian dictator might have dirt on him.

“But I actually think it’s actually larger than that,” Wolff said, floating a very different reason for Trump appearing to admire the Russian leader so much. “What Trump wants... perhaps more than anything, is money. I think Trump in his heart, in his head, wants to be an oligarch.” 

The Trump biographer said that he recently asked a White House insider who is “very close” to Trump how much money the billionaire president hopes to cash in before leaving office. 

“One of the interesting things... about the people around Trump is that they are actually very objective when they talk about him, because he is as foreign to them as Trump is to us,” Wolff said. “I mean, they’re being paid and... they have to fall in line and do all the things... that Trump demands of people. But, you know, they’re clear-eyed.”

Wolff alleged that the White House insider believed Trump was aiming for a $20 billion fortune by the time he leaves office, with deals in place that would allow him and his family to make $100 billion once he returns to Mar-a-Lago.

Trump has made significant headway toward that goal, with his estimated fortune reaching $7 billion in September—about $2.7 billion richer than when he returned to the political spotlight with his 2024 election victory, Forbes reported.

According to Wolff, the White House insider argued that for Trump “it really was about the money, that... being president was nice, but being an oligarch is forever.”

That is at “the root of Trump’s interest in and admiration for Putin, that Putin is the one world leader who has access to the most money with the least amount of regulation,” Wolff argued. 

He suggested Trump’s rift with Ukraine stems from the country’s continued resistance to Putin’s invasion, which has “frustrated” the president’s desire to cut deals and partner with the Russian dictator.

Imagining Trump’s twisted point of view, Wolff said, “So I am now going to do everything possible. I only got two years left, everything possible to close down the Ukraine situation and make deals with Putin.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump’s communications director, Steven Cheung, has previously told the Daily Beast: “Michael Wolff is a lying sack of s--t and has been proven to be a fraud.”

news.title: Todd Blanche Dismisses DOJ’s 60-Day Rule in Virginia Senate Leader Louise Lucas Case Despite Trump’s Past Support
news.text:
The past appears to be repeating itself. Less than two weeks before the midterm elections, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a federal criminal indictment against one of the Republican Party’s most prominent political opponents in Virginia.

The timing of the charges has renewed questions about the Justice Department’s informal “60-day rule,” which advises federal prosecutors and the FBI to avoid announcing charges or taking other conspicuous law enforcement action when it could affect an upcoming election.

The policy is not written into law or formally codified. Instead, it is a longstanding Justice Department norm whose application has often been unclear—and fiercely contested.

On Thursday, at a news conference announcing marijuana, racketeering and money laundering charges against state Sen. Louise Lucas, one of Virginia’s most powerful Democrats, a reporter asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to explain why the indictment was filed so close to Election Day.

“The typical practice is DOJ doesn’t usually release charges like this this close to an election,” the reporter said. “Even though Ms. Lucas is not on the ballot, her daughter is. So can you speak to the reason for the timing of these charges so close to an upcoming election.”

Blanche, the nation’s top law enforcement official, dismissed the concern.

“I think you’re referring to the 60-day or 90-day practice, which is not in writing, that’s not part of the justice manual,” Blanche said. “The justice manual speaks very clearly about what the Department of Justice can and can’t do. And we cannot bring a charge if our purpose is improper. And there’s nothing improper about this purpose.”

Blanche’s response appears to reflect the Trump administration’s current view of the election-year prosecution practice.

In effect, the Justice Department seems to regard the 60-day rule as neither a binding restriction nor a significant factor when bringing charges against political candidates or their immediate relatives. Lucas’ daughter, who is also charged, is running for a seat on the Portsmouth City Council.

President Donald Trump, however, has previously taken a sharply different position—and argued it at considerable length.

Trump has even contended that the appropriate buffer should extend well beyond 60 or 90 days.

In February 2024, then a presidential candidate, Trump argued that special counsel Jack Smith’s investigation into classified documents at Mar-a-Lago was improper because it was proceeding too close to the 2024 election.

Trump’s filing cited a report from the DOJ inspector general concerning former FBI Director James Comey’s well-documented “mistakes” and mishandling during the investigation into Hillary Clinton’s private email server. Among those mistakes was a major law enforcement announcement made just days before Clinton lost the election.

Blanche was the lead attorney on that defense filing, which praised the longstanding tradition against election interference by prosecutors.

Trump also argued that the proposed trial date in the case was unacceptably close to the 2024 election. Smith rejected that argument, maintaining that the relevant action for purposes of the 60-day practice was the indictment itself. Trump had been indicted in the case, which has since been dismissed, in June 2023.

Trump raised the 60-day rule again in August 2024 while criticizing Smith’s prosecution related to Jan. 6. In that instance, Trump objected to a superseding indictment filed within 60 days of the start of early voting for the 2024 election.

news.title: Trump mocks Michigan’s progressive and calls him a ‘jihadist’ as president campaigns in Iowa
news.text:
Donald Trump mocked progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for U.S. Senate in Michigan, and called him a “jihadist” as the president campaigned in Iowa. 

Trump was in Sioux City to stump for Republicans like Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for U.S. Senate against Democrat Josh Turek, after banning The Independent from the trip following the president's attack on reporter Andrew Feinberg earlier in the week.

The president compared Turek to “extremists” such as El-Sayed and Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas and Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

“How about the gentlemen from a place called Michigan? He’s a jihadist,” Trump exclaimed.

El-Sayed, who is Muslim, disavowed the global Islamist organization known as the Muslim Brotherhood at a town hall in Caro, Michigan, over the weekend after being asked to by an attendee if he would do so. But he also asked the man why he would ask such a question. 

“You’re asking the question because implicitly you assume that I’ll have dual loyalties,” El-Sayed said. “You assume that somehow I wouldn’t disavow. Or that I’ll have some higher order, allegiance than to the Constitution.”

Trump was campaigning in Sioux City for Hinson and Zach Lahn, who is running for Iowa governor against Democrat Rob Sand.

Both Hinson and Lahn’s races remain tight in a state that Trump won in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential elections. Turek is leading Hinson 48 to 45 percent, while Sand is ahead of Lahn 52 to 45 percent among likely voters in Iowa, according to a recent Marist Poll. 

Feinberg, White House correspondent for The Independent, was supposed to travel with Trump to Sioux City on Air Force One — until he got on the president’s bad side for asking questions the president didn’t like during an Oval Office event Tuesday. At one point during the event, Trump called Feinberg a “sick person” and said, “I actually think there’s something wrong with you.”

Feinberg, a member of the traveling White House press pool, was notified by the White House Press Office Wednesday evening that he will “not be the print pooler on tomorrow’s trip,” despite his scheduled shift in the rotation being confirmed days earlier. 

“The anonymous email did not say why, but it was obvious that I was being punished for what happened on Tuesday,” Feinberg wrote in a new article about his experience being booted from the president’s jet. “I’m not there to be friendly with this president or administration. And guess what? I wasn’t there to be friendly with the last one, either.”

“There will be an administration after this one. It may well be one with a Democratic president in the Oval Office once more,” Feinberg said. “And I’ll be there, doing the exact same thing.”

Trump has made it his mission to get voters to turn out for Republican candidates, telling his supporters to pretend that he’s on the ballot. The president has gone so far as to promise $5,000 checks to Americans if Republicans keep control of Congress, which critics have called a bribe. 

Meanwhile, Trump’s rallies meant to drum up excitement among his base have been constantly interrupted by the yells of protesters. The president has tried to combat his hecklers with “your mom” and fat jokes. 

At a rally in North Carolina earlier this week, Trump went as far as to compare the hecklers to rioters in Paris, who have spread violence during nationwide protests over the rising cost of living and poor conditions of schools in France. 

As Trump tries to boost GOP candidates’ chances of winning the midterms, he has his own image issue to deal with. The president has hit a record low approval rating of 33 percent in a new ABC New/Washington Post/Ipsos poll.

His administration has been dogged by an unpopular war in Iran, stubborn inflation and an immigration crackdown that most Americans have found too aggressive.
news.summary: Trump went after Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico and Ilhan Omar at his rally in Sioux City, Iowa, as he stumps for Republicans ahead of November’s midterms

news.text:
Donald Trump is hanging out to dry a former adviser who is now the subject of a Justice Department inquiry.

Trump, before flying to a midterm rally in Iowa, spoke at the White House about the inquiry into Corey Lewandowski, who was the top adviser to ex-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem until their March ouster. Lewandowksi, 53, is alleged to have profited off of his role, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. He denies the claims.

“No, I don’t know about it. I mean, I heard something about it. But I don’t know exactly what it is. All I know is, I want my people to be honest, and if they’re not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted,” Trump, 80, said. “I don’t know about specifically, but—because I view it [if] people are not honest, they’re stealing from me, as president. They’re stealing from me. So, I want my people to be honest, and if they’re not honest, I’ll have my DOJ go and do whatever they have to do.”

A reporter followed up: “It sounds like you’re okay with that investigation, then?” 

“Well, I—I—I guess I could stop anything,” Trump said. “Look, if my people are not—I have no idea what he did. I have—just heard about it a little while. I want the people that work for this administration to be 100 percent honest.”

The inquiry into Lewandowski, who has been an inner Trumpworld figure for the past decade, was spurred by a referral from the DHS inspector general, according to the Journal. It wasn’t immediately clear which alleged actions by Lewandowski were included in the referral, but the Journal reported last month that the inspector general was looking into how he appeared to use his stature in the administration to enrich himself, for instance by asking Qatari and U.A.E. officials to hire him on the side to help with issues like visas. Some of the foreign officials were reportedly “taken aback” by Lewandowski’s alleged offer.

Lewandowski—or close associates of his—also approved nearly all DHS expenditures over $100,000, the Journal notes, meaning he was in a position to know about DHS’ many contractors. 

Lewandowski denies wrongdoing. His attorney, Adam Trigg, told the Daily Beast in a statement: “Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity.”

A DOJ spokesperson declined to comment to the Daily Beast.

Neither Trigg nor Lewandowski immediately responded when asked about Trump’s reaction to the inquiry.

The Journal previously reported that Lewandowski told allies that he expects a Trump pardon should any criminal charges be brought. His lawyer denied this.

The inquiry is the first instance—in public, at least—of Trump’s second-term Justice Department looking into an individual in the president’s orbit.

Lewandowski was Trump’s presidential campaign manager from 2015 until June 2016, and was a senior adviser to his 2024 campaign.

While at DHS, Lewandowski’s alleged affair with Noem was described as the “worst-kept secret” in D.C.

news.title: Trump Says Musk Restored Ukraine’s Starshield
news.text:
US President Donald Trump said Thursday, Oct. 22, that Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s military-grade Starshield satellite communications service following restrictions that disrupted Ukrainian drone operations, but declined to confirm whether he personally called the billionaire to demand the changes be reversed.

“I don’t want to comment on it, you know, whether I called or whether somebody else called – doesn’t make any difference,” Trump told reporters when asked about a Wall Street Journal report that he had intervened.

“I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk, whose SpaceX company operates the satellite network.

Trump’s comments followed a Wall Street Journal investigation reporting that the president contacted Musk on Wednesday and asked him to remove restrictions that had sharply reduced Ukraine’s ability to operate certain military drones.

According to the newspaper, citing US officials, Trump expressed frustration that the service remained capped at approximately 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour), a restriction that interfered with communications aboard fast-moving Ukrainian drones.

US and Ukrainian officials cited by the Journal said network performance improved after the reported conversation. However, some Ukrainian officials cautioned that the service had not returned to full functionality.

The latest developments leave a central question unresolved: whether Ukraine has regained the satellite communications capabilities it needs to conduct strikes against Russian military targets and intercept incoming drones.

Restrictions disrupted Ukrainian strike and interceptor drones

The controversy began on Oct. 14, when Ukrainian military units reported unexpected limitations on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network.

Unlike ordinary Starlink terminals, Starshield supports specialized military communications and can be used aboard high-speed unmanned aircraft.

Ukraine relies on the system for battlefield coordination, strikes against Russian military positions in occupied territory, reconnaissance and interceptor drones designed to destroy incoming Russian attack drones.

The sudden speed restrictions caused terminals to lose connectivity aboard moving platforms, disrupting missions and limiting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian aerial attacks.
news.summary: President Donald Trump says Elon Musk restored Ukraine’s military-grade Starshield satellite service after speed restrictions disrupted Ukrainian strike and interceptor drones. The US president declined to confirm reports that he personally intervened.

news.title: Russia bombs Kyiv, Ukraine fires drones towards Moscow
news.text:
KYIV: Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US push to end the conflict.

Russia said on Wednesday it was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, after President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in St Petersburg.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he hoped negotiations, which would be the first since February, would take place early in November.

Ukraine said Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles in three waves, and Zelenskiy said three of them carried cluster munitions — “bomblets” that disperse over a wide area and are banned by many countries because of the danger they pose to civilians. Russia’s defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards Moscow during the night.

The two sides held an exchange of war dead, with Moscow handing over 252 bodies and Ukraine handing over 25, according to the Belta state news agency in neighbouring Belarus. Such exchanges have accompanied moves towards talks in the past.

But while Witkoff spoke of “some degree of momentum” after meeting Zelenskiy and European and NATO officials in Oslo earlier in the week, the Kremlin expressed doubts.

“The Americans sensed some new nuances (in Oslo) and told us about this. But these nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.

A senior Russian official, briefed on the results of the Putin-Witkoff talks, said they were relatively short and not substantive. The American brought a set of proposals drafted in Oslo and handed them to Putin for review, the person said.

Another source close to the Kremlin said the US proposals included a scenario where Ukraine would cede all of its Donbas region to Russia in return for receiving a guarantee of its future security from NATO.

Russia says it launched the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two, in part to prevent Ukraine from joining NATO. It has repeatedly said it would not end fighting unless Ukraine cedes more land, limits the size of its forces and is permanently barred from forming alliances.

Ukraine, which says the invasion was an unprovoked war of conquest, has long dismissed Russia’s conditions as a demand for capitulation that would leave it defenceless against future Russian attacks.

US praise for ‘humanitarian’ Putin goes down badly with Kyiv

Zelenskiy’s meeting with Witkoff was aimed in part at smoothing over a deterioration in relations with Washington this month, after President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and lifted sanctions on Moscow.

Kyiv says Washington failed to provide early-warning data on Russian missile launches, throttled the SpaceX satellite system used to guide Ukrainian drones, and withheld missile defence systems bought on its behalf by Europeans. Washington denies any shift in policy to intentionally hamper Ukraine’s forces.

Trump has repeatedly rebuked Ukraine for attacking Russian oil refineries while saying little about far deadlier Russian attacks on Ukraine. He called for Zelenskiy to be replaced and said Russia’s actions in Ukraine have been “fine”.

Zelenskiy, who long avoided any criticism of the Trump administration, has increasingly pushed back against what he describes as a shift towards sympathy with Moscow.

On Thursday Zelenskiy snapped back at Witkoff for saluting Putin as a “humanitarian” during his visit to Russia, when the US envoy thanked Putin for releasing a 74-year-old American captured by Russian forces in Ukraine.

“Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening,” Zelenskiy posted on X. “They used 21 missiles. Unfortunately, numerous sites across the city have been hit and damaged.”

He said 2 people were killed and 34 injured, including 5 children, in attacks on a dozen Ukrainian regions.

Russia said it carried out a “massive strike” overnight on port infrastructure in Ukraine’s Odesa region, as well as on vessels used by the Ukrainian military.

In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow by drones launched towards the capital during the night, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added.

In the Russian border region of Belgorod, one man was killed and another wounded by Ukrainian drones, local officials said.

With the frontlines of the war largely static, both sides have escalated long-range air strikes this year. Russia has particularly targeted the Ukrainian power grid, while Ukraine has aimed at Russian oil refineries. Both have struck data centres, commercial warehouses and Black Sea shipping.

The war has ground on for more than 4-1/2 years, defying Trump’s pledge during his 2024 election campaign that he could end it in a day. No breakthrough emerged from three short meetings in Istanbul last year and three rounds of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi and Geneva at the start of this year.

news.title: Four in five immigrants deported under Trump 2.0 have no criminal record, study finds
news.text:
RIYADH: Of the 980,000 migrants deported during the first 18 months of US President Donald Trump’s second term, only 20 percent were individuals with a criminal conviction, according to a report published on Thursday by the Migration Policy Institute think tank.

The study, authored by Marc Rosenblum, a former head of the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Homeland Security Statistics, provides one of the most comprehensive assessments of immigration enforcement under Trump’s second administration.

The report found that the US Department of Homeland Security, through Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), carried out about 980,000 deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026.

Only around 190,000 of those deported had criminal convictions, despite Trump’s repeated pledges to target what he has described as “the worst of the worst” criminals living in the United States.

Majority of deportees had no criminal convictions

According to the report, 80 percent of all deportations during the period involved people with no criminal record.

Among immigrants who had lived in the United States for two years or more, 71 percent of those deported had no criminal conviction. The trend also extended to long-term residents, with 61 percent of deportees who had lived in the country for a decade or longer having no criminal record.

Even among formal removals, where criminal offenders have traditionally represented a larger share of deportees, only 31 percent had criminal convictions. The report said that was significantly lower than the 44 percent average recorded between fiscal years 2009 and 2021.

The findings suggest that immigration enforcement has increasingly focused on migrants living inside the country rather than on recent border arrivals.

Deportations rise but remain below early-2000s levels

The report said annual deportation levels under Trump’s second term have surpassed those recorded during former President Joe Biden’s administration and Trump’s first term.

However, deportations remain well below the levels routinely seen during the early 2000s.

Of the nearly 980,000 deportations recorded during the first 18 months of Trump’s second term, about 580,000 were classified as removals, 300,000 as enforcement returns and 110,000 as administrative returns.

The study also found a sharp increase in immigration arrests within the US interior. Deportations stemming from interior arrests rose from around 8,000 per month in early 2025 to about 19,000 per month by mid-2026, accounting for nearly 40 percent of all deportations nationwide.

Meanwhile, encounters along the US-Mexico border have fallen to historically low levels, shifting enforcement priorities deeper into the country, according to the report.

Expanded enforcement apparatus

The findings come as the Trump administration has significantly expanded immigration enforcement resources.

Congress approved $240 billion in immigration enforcement funding for DHS through fiscal year 2029, enabling ICE to hire an additional 12,000 officers, more than doubling the agency’s operational workforce.

The administration has also increasingly relied on voluntary departures and enforcement returns to speed up removals and avoid heavily backlogged immigration courts.

According to the report, about 170,000 deportations involved ICE grants of voluntary departure or return, a record level that allowed migrants to leave without going through formal deportation proceedings.

The study also questioned administration claims that more than three million immigrants have left the country through a combination of deportations and voluntary “self-deportations.” Researchers estimated total departures of immigrants who had lived in the US for at least one year at between 790,000 and 1.9 million.

Debate over crackdown continues

Trump has argued that his immigration crackdown and deportation campaign are necessary to improve public safety and enforce immigration laws.

The administration says expanded interior arrests help restore the rule of law and deter illegal immigration.

Civil rights groups and immigration advocates have sharply criticized the policies, arguing that they have eroded due process protections, fostered fear among immigrant communities and increased concerns about racial profiling.

The administration’s immigration measures have faced multiple legal challenges with mixed outcomes in US courts.

Separately, the State Department said this week that the Trump administration has revoked more than 300,000 US visas during the president’s second term.

Among the revocations criticized by rights advocates were those involving pro-Palestinian demonstrators protesting Israel’s war in Gaza and foreigners whose social media posts referred to the assassination of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk.

Hello, as I write this, the latest news about your great-granddad is that a court of law has ruled a police raid on his residence illegal. Nonetheless, the police rationalise the illegal act and surprisingly say they wish to use the materials they seized as evidence in court. If this isn’t a scenario of “we must nail him by all means”, I don’t know what it is. Note that this is the first time a matter concerning allegations made against your great-granddad comes before their Lordships for determination, and he wins. This should give you an impression of the world in which your great -granddad happened. Everyone, including the police, appears to want to capitalise on his situation so badly that they engage in illegal acts or breach professional ethics. There’s this frenzy to convict him in the court of public opinion in a nation where citizens are presumed innocent until found guilty.

This piece is the other side to whatever you’ve read about your great-granddad. I know it’s a different world you meet, isn’t it? To me, it’s different only in the tools used. Humans, especially their emotional instincts, remain the same across the ages. In spite of whatever has transpired, for instance, your great-granddad’s mother loves him as mothers have always loved their children. Many people across the world like your great-granddad, too, one reason being that he has this naturally likable personality. In any case, the Yoruba people of Nigeria say, “one’s child can’t be so bad that one gives him to the leopard to kill”. I like and respect your great-granddad. Then news of mistakes in choosing friends came. Is it possible to suddenly dislike one’s child, or someone one feels close to, like one’s blood brother? I shall illustrate my point. Many years ago I travelled to a town, and on one of those days I embarked on my daily keep-fit walk. About two hundred metres ahead I noticed this large crowd in front of a prison facility. The crowd was such that it spilled onto the expressway and prison officials had to animatedly engage in some crowd control.

Despite such treatment from prison officials, the people, many of whom carried containers that one would suspect contained food, wouldn’t go away. I wondered why they were there. I later discovered it was visiting day. No matter the offence their sons, daughters, brothers, sisters, fathers or mothers had committed, these relatives and friends didn’t abandon them. That’s humans for you – emotional, compassionate. Humans don’t abandon those who’re really their own. That day, I took a different route, understanding that people needed to be forgiven for blocking the road for a few hours to show they cared about their own, even if the rest of the world distanced itself. I’ve never met your great-granddad, but if you get the point in my illustration, you’ll understand why some of us won’t dislike him just because allegations are made against him. Note that many who’re unforgiving towards your great-granddad do go to prisons to show care and sympathy for their convicted relatives and friends, waiting for them to come out and get a second chance.

Meanwhile, it may interest you to know that there are many who reason and talk like the then Archbishop of Canterbury once did, even if their voices don’t make it to the tabloids because it’s not popularly ‘correct’ to have them there. The archbishop said your great-granddad told him that he would like to make up for some incorrect choices he made in the past (“Archbishop Welby speaks for Prince Andrew and humanity”, ’Tunji Ajibade, The PUNCH, Aug. 22, 2022). The archbishop’s focus, I believe, is reconciliation and reconciliation is vertical as well as horizontal, something I pointed out in the quoted column. Many who realise that the archbishop’s job is essentially to reconcile understand and agree with him.

Back to your great-granddad’s mother who never abandoned him; you may think that’s only natural, and I agree. But it also indicated to me she didn’t think her son was the worst of humans, and I agree too. You see, many issues conspired against your great-granddad to pile up in those materials you’ve read. Among them, it’s the state of our world I call attention to. Most people make something out of another person’s situation, especially personalities like your great-granddad. Those in uniform aren’t left out. By admitting they consciously adopted illegal means to search his residence, as made clear in their official response to court ruling, the police have joined others in making stick on your great-granddad the “un-stickable”. Making stick the “un-stickable” is a main feature of your great-grandfather’s situation, as nothing he’s accused of has thus far been proven in a court of law. I presume if a court hadn’t declared their act illegal, some officers would have gotten away with the act of illegality, and their profiles would later proudly read in bold letters that they were part of the team that raided Andrew Mountbatten Windsor’s residence. Some profit from other people’s situation, and it’s one reason our world is so unforgiving.

As for talk of objective and balanced reporting, none of such applied in your great-granddad’s case. Every news report or opinion piece starts with the “disgraced” prince. There must be a clear negative qualifier because readers must know straightaway that reporters share their judgmental disposition, even though the profession requires them to report issues without value judgement. Everyone in the profession bows to something, including the audience, whose preferences must be reinforced. Note that your great-granddad isn’t the only victim of the world we live in, a world that believes a person is guilty by association. Yet those who believe this have kids and friends convicted for serious offences and they themselves aren’t guilty by association.

Here’s the backdrop to those materials you read about your great-granddad. After a certain US businessman died in jail before standing trial for his offences, everyone ever associated with him was asked to answer for what they knew and what they didn’t know. There were wild allegations made against those who had the briefest of encounters with the businessman. The US president, Donald Trump with the First Lady, has had to publicly respond to such wild allegations that are basically the imagination of some people’s mind. Another former US president, Bill Clinton and his wife Hillary, responded to questions too. This makes me ask: if the businessman didn’t die, would such a net have been cast to get his associates to answer in his stead? There’s is this sense of “grab whoever is alive and make them pay” to this hunt. Most prominent people dragged into this have since been left alone except your great-grandfather, and there’s a reason for it. His name, his status, as a senior member of the royal family sells news; even long after the news is dead, he can resurrect it. Such is how some reporters have any attention-grabbing news to submit to their editors, how some opinion piece writers get paid.

Your great-granddad admitted he made the mistake, like many other personalities stated, of being in contact with the said businessman and he apologised. As for allegations made by some, your great-granddad said it was long ago and he couldn’t recall details about those who made allegations. He apologised, had the matter settled out of court, and compensation paid, which was the responsible thing to do. The allegation that he shares secret information as the nation’s trade ambassador has yet to be proven in court. Worth noting, though, is that at the time he told the archbishop he wanted to mend his ways, many who would ask for forgiveness and expect to be forgiven for their own mistakes rebuffed him. That’s the world in which your great-granddad happened. Never think the worst of him; he’s a gentleman that many of us like, and we wish he never had contact with the businessman whose other ulterior motives were obviously not your great granddad’s.

Until the story of his contact with the businessman emerged, your great-granddad was dutiful, respectable, a great personality, and an asset to the royal family, which is why his mother stood by him. Now one wrong choice of friend he made is seized by everyone to summarise his entire life. Such shouldn’t happen. After you must have read some revelations about prominent news hunters who relentlessly rend his image, but who were later found to have something to hide themselves, I imagine you would judge your great-granddad more appropriately. Beyond this, I think reconciliation that’s vertical, which the archbishop inferred that your great-granddad equally sought, is important too in a world that’s become so decidedly unforgiving.

news.title: Netanyahu helped Kushner hide $1 billion in UAE funds at Israel's central bank, book claims
news.text: A secret network of bank accounts allegedly connected Jared Kushner, senior adviser to President Donald Trump, with powerful Gulf rulers and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during Trump's first term, according to allegations detailed in a forthcoming book by investigative journalist Matthew Cole, excerpts of which were published by Vanity Fair. The book claims that at least $2 billion was made available through financial arrangements spanning the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Israel, including an alleged $1 billion transfer to an account at Israel's central bank. Kushner's lawyer categorically denied the alleged arrangements. The claims appear in Cole's book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East. According to Cole's account, Emirati leader Mohamed bin Zayed and Saudi Arabia's Mohammed bin Salman initially discussed establishing a fund exceeding $10 billion to advance political objectives important to the incoming Trump administration. The plan reportedly narrowed into several accounts allegedly giving Kushner access to foreign funds outside conventional U.S. government oversight. One of the most significant allegations concerns approximately $1 billion that bin Zayed allegedly transferred to Israel through Azerbaijan in 2018. Citing a person briefed on the arrangement, Cole writes that Netanyahu encouraged Kushner to place the money in an account at the Bank of Israel, where it would appear to be associated with government funds rather than with Kushner personally. The source claimed the money was intended for Kushner's personal benefit, although the book excerpt does not establish how the funds were ultimately used. The Bank of Israel does not operate personal accounts, and government accounts require authorization from two individuals to conduct transactions. According to Cole, Netanyahu wanted Kushner to inform him before any transfers, with messages allegedly conveyed through David Friedman, then the U.S. ambassador to Israel. One source claimed that significant sums were subsequently transferred through Cyprus. Friedman emphatically denied any knowledge of the alleged arrangement or involvement in transmitting messages, while Kushner's lawyer insisted that "there are no accounts and never were." How Dutch intelligence allegedly uncovered the financial trail Cole traces the alleged financial network to an extraordinary intelligence operation that began in late 2017, when the Netherlands' military intelligence service reportedly discovered that a hacker working for Russia's GRU military intelligence agency was preparing to travel to Britain. With British cooperation, Dutch intelligence officers allegedly persuaded the operative to provide access to a Russian intelligence server rather than face arrest. Investigators reviewing material on that server reportedly discovered screenshots from Kushner's iPhone, prompting an effort to determine how Russian hackers had compromised the device. By early 2018, Dutch cyber specialists had allegedly found a vulnerability that allowed them to monitor images appearing on Kushner's screen as he used his phone. According to the book, the surveillance revealed that Kushner was accessing a UAE bank account that had received hundreds of millions of dollars through an Azerbaijani bank. The account, identified by Cole as Alpha, was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank and had allegedly received approximately $750 million beginning in 2017, with funding attributed to Saudi and Emirati sources. The use of Azerbaijan was particularly significant, Cole argues, because certain banks there allegedly facilitate large foreign-currency transfers that obscure the original source of the funds. Rather than transferring Saudi riyals or Emirati dirhams directly to their destination, clients could reportedly use intermediary transactions that delivered equivalent amounts in U.S. dollars. For investigators examining the final transfer, the money could appear to originate from an Azerbaijani institution, concealing the financial arrangements behind it. The Alpha account was allegedly held by the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, an Emirati government-funded charity, rather than by Kushner personally. Cole alleges that Kushner was made an authorized signatory, giving him potential access to the funds without formal ownership. The foundation, headed at the time by Dherar Belhoul Al Falasi, allegedly served another purpose: facilitating covert Emirati arms purchases and foreign operations. A confidential source cited by Cole described the charity as a vehicle that could reduce scrutiny of sensitive transactions. Kushner's lawyer denied that his client knew Al Falasi, had any connection to the foundation or possessed access to a UAE bank account. According to Cole, the alleged financial arrangements developed alongside ambitious diplomatic plans involving Washington, Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Jerusalem. Mohammed bin Salman was seeking to consolidate his position as Saudi crown prince, while bin Zayed wanted the Trump administration to abandon Barack Obama's nuclear agreement with Iran. Kushner, meanwhile, was pursuing an Israeli-Palestinian peace initiative and closer relations between Israel and Gulf states. The book alleges that access to the funds was connected to those overlapping political objectives, although the precise terms of any arrangement remain disputed. Israeli security arrangements and questions of oversight Cole's book also describes a third, separate account allegedly established during secret contacts between Israel and the UAE before the countries formally normalized diplomatic relations in 2020. Kushner reportedly helped negotiate an understanding under which Israel would assist the Emirates in defending against a major Iranian military attack. According to Cole, Abu Dhabi deposited additional money into an Israeli central bank account to finance such emergency assistance. The excerpt does not specify the amount involved or establish whether the funds were ever used. Cole argues that the three alleged accounts effectively created an unofficial financial framework through which Kushner could pursue Middle East diplomacy with senior regional leaders. The arrangements, if substantiated, would raise questions about transparency and government oversight. Kushner was an unpaid senior White House adviser but remained a federal employee subject to financial disclosure requirements, including obligations associated with access to classified information. Cole says four former senior Trump administration officials, including national security advisers and a former CIA director, were unaware of presidential authorization for Kushner to access a foreign government account. The book excerpt also examines potential legal implications. A former prosecutor who worked on Robert Mueller's investigation told Cole that any agreement to provide official influence in exchange for money could potentially violate federal bribery laws or foreign-agent registration requirements. Such an assessment depends on whether the alleged arrangements existed and what, if anything, was promised in return. The allegations presented in the book do not amount to a judicial finding that Kushner committed a crime, and his attorney denied any legal violations or undisclosed financial arrangements. Kushner's counsel maintained that his dealings with foreign officials were conducted with Trump's approval and in the interests of the United States. Friedman separately rejected the allegations involving him as entirely false. The competing accounts leave major questions unresolved, including whether the reported bank accounts existed as described, who controlled the funds and whether any money was used for personal purposes. Cole's account, published in excerpt form by Vanity Fair, nevertheless places the alleged financial relationships at the center of the diplomatic efforts that preceded the Abraham Accords, raising questions about whether an undisclosed system of financial arrangements operated alongside official U.S. Middle East policy.
news.summary: US journalist Matthew Cole alleges Netanyahu urged Kushner to move Emirati funds into a Bank of Israel account as part of a $2 billion concealment effort, and demanded advance notice of transfers; Kushner rejects the claims as ‘completely insane’
news.author: Daniel Edelson, New York

news.title: Macron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France
news.text:
French President Emmanuel Macron has announced a crackdown on public demonstrations, ordering authorities to ban protests deemed “illegitimate” and restrict even officially organized marches as nationwide unrest over soaring living costs and deteriorating public services continues.

The restrictions, announced Thursday following an emergency meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, come ahead of another wave of demonstrations planned for Saturday, after some of France’s worst street violence in years.

Macron said local authorities would prohibit gatherings organized by individuals or groups deemed to lack legitimate authority, while demonstrations arranged by recognized organizations, such as trade unions, would be considered for approval but could be forced onto alternative routes.

“The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days,” Macron declared, insisting the measures were necessary to restore calm and protect businesses and public buildings.

“Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic,” he claimed, accusing organized radicals of orchestrating violence and looting.

The announcement significantly tightens restrictions on public gatherings in a country where the right to protest is constitutionally protected. Under French law, authorities can prohibit demonstrations on public-order grounds, although such decisions must be proportionate and can be challenged in court.

A Paris administrative court overturned a police ban on a student demonstration on Thursday, allowing thousands of protesters to gather despite official objections. The rally proceeded peacefully under heavy police presence, according to AP.

However, authorities have already prohibited Saturday’s demonstrations in central Lyon, where hundreds of businesses were ransacked last weekend. Similar restrictions have been imposed in Marseille, Nice and Toulon. In Paris, one authorized march has been diverted away from the city center, while another involving students and members of the Yellow Vest movement has been banned.

France has been gripped by escalating unrest since protests over teacher shortages and deteriorating school conditions spread into a broader movement against rising prices, inequality and cuts to public services.

Around 550,000 people joined demonstrations last Saturday, which descended into clashes with police, arson and widespread looting. Nearly 2,500 people have since been arrested, while approximately 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, according to figures reported by French media.

Opposition leaders have blamed Macron’s policies and failure to maintain order for the crisis. National Rally leader Marine Le Pen described him as a president “without credibility or authority” who has “lost all touch with reality,” while left-wing leader Jean-Luc Melenchon accused his government of undermining public services over the past decade.

Even police unions have turned against the administration. Alliance Police Nationale announced plans to sue the state, accusing officials of abandoning officers during the riots and failing to provide adequate equipment and clear instructions.

Macron has also clashed with US President Donald Trump, who blamed France’s turmoil on uncontrolled immigration and radical groups. The French leader dismissed comments by foreign politicians about the unrest as “stupid” and “unacceptable.”

The president is expected to chair another emergency defense council meeting on Friday to decide whether further restrictions are needed ahead of Saturday’s protests.
news.summary:
President Emmanuel Macron has announced a crackdown on public demonstrations, ordering authorities to ban protests deemed “illegitimate”

news.title: Trump Reacts After Rep. Ilhan Omar Denies Marrying Her Brother
news.text:
Donald Trump said Ilhan Omar’s response to a question about whether she married her brother sounded like a startling admission.

The 44-year-old Minnesota congresswoman faced the question days after federal agents searched her Washington, DC, home in connection with an investigation into alleged immigration fraud.

Trump, who has clashed with Omar for years, said he found it unusual that she used the words “not to my knowledge” during an interview outside the White House on Thursday.

“If you asked me that same question about, let’s say, my sister, I would say ‘no.’ She said ‘not to my knowledge.’ That tells you a lot right there,” Trump said.

Trump acknowledged that he has “never been a big fan of hers” and urged people to “see how it works out” as the investigation continues.

He again insisted that Omar’s wording was significant, saying, “That statement tells you a lot.”

Omar rejected the long-running allegations as “insane” and accused right-wing influencers of helping circulate the conspiracy theories.

MS NOW host Chris Hayes asked Omar whether there was even a remote possibility that she was related to her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.

“You were not related to him at all? There’s not a weird kernel of truth…” Hayes asked.

“Not to my knowledge,” Omar replied.

The exchange took place during Omar’s first major interview since Homeland Security Investigations seized phones, computers and other personal belongings from her home.

Hayes introduced the subject by noting the extraordinary nature of the accusations, which Trump and other political opponents have repeatedly amplified.

“There are right-wing people who believe that this man was your brother. You have called it a disgusting lie,” Hayes told the congresswoman.

“Who was this man who was your husband? When did they start saying that he was your brother? Why?” he asked, referring to her former husband.

Omar said the allegation began on a Somali blog before conservative activists in Minneapolis picked it up.

“It started with the Somali blog. I don’t know if it still exists, but somebody put in there that, you know, he had to have been my brother or something to that effect. And right-wing conspiracy theorists in Minneapolis got hold of it,” she said.

‘And they just kind of went and found random people who were like, she introduced us. She introduced him to us and said he was her brother, which is, you know, insane. I mean, I don’t know those people that they talk about.’

Hayes then pressed the congresswoman on whether there was any truth to the allegations. 

Omar accused her critics of finding supposed witnesses who claimed she had introduced Elmi as her sibling.

‘They just kind of went and found random people who were like, “She introduced us. She introduced him to us and said he was her brother,” which is, you know, insane.’

Omar insisted she did not recognize the individuals making those claims.

There is no established evidence that Elmi is Omar’s brother, and the congresswoman has consistently denied the allegation.

The interview also provided Omar’s most detailed account yet of the dramatic federal search that has placed her citizenship and personal affairs under intense scrutiny.

She claimed approximately 15 to 25 agents arrived at her residence at 6am, pounding on doors while she and her family were asleep.

‘I only had two and a half hours of sleep when they came, you know, pounding on the doors,’ she recalled.

Omar said she initially feared an emergency was unfolding outside.

‘I thought something was on fire. I thought something was happening to the neighbors,’ she explained.

The congresswoman said agents spent between four and five hours searching the property, eventually removing 17 items, including several phones, notebooks, a vintage camera and a Somali language book.

She described the operation as ‘intrusive but polite,’ acknowledging that agents treated her belongings carefully and even folded some of her clothes.

Nevertheless, she accused the Trump administration of orchestrating an intimidating spectacle designed to satisfy the president’s supporters.

‘They had to do something, I believe, to say, hey, look, we raided her house,’ she alleged.

Federal investigators are examining possible immigration fraud, with the Minnesota US Attorney’s Office investigating whether false statements were made in immigration documents concerning Omar’s birth date.

Investigators have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including some involving Omar’s relatives.

The congresswoman maintains that she legally obtained American citizenship at 17 through her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, who became a naturalized citizen in 2000.

She suggested investigators were now focusing on documents completed by her late father, who can no longer defend himself.

‘It’s also very convenient because my dad is no longer alive,’ Omar told Hayes. ‘So it’s another thing they can drag on forever.’

Trump has publicly suggested Omar could face imprisonment if investigators establish that she committed immigration fraud.

‘She could go to jail,’ the president said on Tuesday. ‘They keep talking about deportation.’

Omar, however, insisted she had committed no wrongdoing and accused the administration of pursuing a politically motivated campaign against her.

She also addressed separate questions surrounding her family’s finances after congressional disclosure documents appeared to value business interests connected to her husband, Tim Mynett, at approximately $30 million.

That figure was subsequently revised substantially downward, with Hayes saying liabilities reduced the reported valuation to around $20,000.

Omar rejected suggestions that she was secretly wealthy, portraying herself as an ordinary working American struggling with everyday expenses.

‘I mean, it’s, you know, working, working class, I guess, like paycheck to paycheck still,’ she said.

‘We’ve got four kids. And, you know, we live, I think, like a basic life.’

She pointed to the family’s modest vehicle as evidence.

‘I have a Toyota Camry that’s from 2016. It’s our only car. I rent my DC place and my Minneapolis place.’

Omar also revealed that she intends to leave her Washington residence after its address became public following the search.

Citing the death threats she regularly receives, she said remaining at the property would endanger her family’s privacy and security.

‘I can’t continue to live there,’ she declared.

Despite the mounting legal and political pressure, Omar insisted she would not be driven out of Congress.

She claimed the president’s ultimate objective was to force her from public office, arguing that her opponents resented someone of her background and faith holding political power.

‘I think that’s ultimately the thing that they want,’ she said.

news.title: Calley Means, a key MAHA advocate, resigns as a top RFK Jr. adviser
news.text:
Calley Means, a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a chief advocate for the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from his position with the Trump administration Thursday.

In a statement, Means did not say why he was leaving. His departure comes as leading voices in the MAHA movement have expressed discontent with what they say is the Trump administration’s lack of progress on a variety of issues, including food security and regulating the weed killer glyphosate.

Means said he “leaves with tremendous respect” for President Donald Trump and Kennedy. 

“The past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and healthcare incentives that profit from us being sick,” Means said. “This movement is in the first inning and just getting started.”

Means was hired as a White House adviser early in the second Trump administration. He used his perch at the Health and Human Services Department to attack the nation’s leading physician groups, federal agencies and government scientists, claiming they only protect their own interests.

White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration is “grateful” for Means’ time and “he has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement.” A representative from Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment. 

Health activist Kelly Ryerson, a leader of American Regeneration who is also known as Glyphosate Girl on social media, said she is “impressed that he completed over two years at HHS fighting the food battle, despite all of the obstacles presented by corporate interests.”

“At the heart of MAHA is a shared belief that the nation’s health must not be sacrificed to corporate profit, and that a preventable slide into chronic disease is a threat to America itself,” she said.

Means is the brother of wellness influencer, author and entrepreneur Dr. Casey Means, who failed to be confirmed as surgeon general earlier this year after doubts were raised over her vaccine stance.

Means, along with his sister, came to prominence within the MAHA movement by arguing that ultraprocessed foods, additives and pesticides could be blamed for many of the chronic health conditions facing Americans.

Means brought those arguments into the Trump administration and frequently clashed with senior White House officials who worried about alienating the powerful food industry.

At the same time, Means’ emphasis on food was a source of frustration for other figures within the MAHA movement who wanted to see Kennedy focus on “medical freedom” issues. For many, that meant rolling back federal recommendations and approvals for vaccines.

Despite Means’ efforts, the administration’s progress on food reforms has been slow going.

Kennedy had promised the release of a first-ever government definition of ultraprocessed food in April. Instead, FDA’s acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, told a conference that month that defining the class “is really hard.”

In August, Kennedy staffers again suggested a major announcement on the issue was imminent. Instead, the announcement focused on a proposal bringing greater scrutiny to food additives. It made only passing mention of ultraprocessed foods.

Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America, said Means will be missed by her organization, which operates local and national campaigns warning against pollution, water use and electricity costs associated with data center construction. 

Honeycutt said Means “brought an energy and fearlessness to the Hill, fighting for our children to have healthy food in schools and for America’s health.”
news.summary: A leading advocate for the Make America Healthy Again movement has resigned as a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Calley Means says he leaves with respect for President Donald Trump and Kennedy

news.title: Karoline Leavitt breaks silence on her replacement Katie Zacharia's sudden firing by Trump
news.text: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has commented after her replacement was fired after just five days on the job. Leavitt also said she offered to help US President Donald Trump choose "someone who can serve him and the country well". Mr Trump sacked his new press secretary Katie Zacharia on Friday, October 16 after one briefing and mounting questions over her qualifications. She was appointed on Monday, October 12. The departure has left the US president without a public messenger just over two weeks before November's midterm elections . Speaking with FOX News Digital's Paul Steinhauser, Ms Leavitt said, "Well, look, White House Press Secretary is a tough job. "I know that because I did it, obviously, for almost two years. And many people say it's one of the hardest jobs in politics." Ms Leavitt said the job "takes a lot of preparation." She added: "And sometimes you don't know how someone will perform until they go out there. "So, look, as the president said, we wish Katie the best. The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well. "And I think - I know the President is continuing to look over options." Mr Trump's former spokesperson said the role is highly sought-after. She added that she had "offered my help to the President to help him select someone who can serve him and the country well." Asked what advice she would give if the US leader if he asked for it, Ms Leavitt was evasive. "Well, I'll keep my private counsel to the President private," she said. "But I do obviously talk to him about what the job entails, and he knows it very well," she added. "Nobody understands the press better than Donald Trump." According to Leavitt, the president needs someone who "is tough, who is smart, who understands his policies, who is loyal, and who can go out there and put up a fight." "There's a lot of qualified people who can have it," Leavitt continued. "It's just up to the president to make that decision." Mr Trump said last week that he had asked Ms Zacharia to "reconsider" her position within his administration after a messy first week. According to Trump, the decision was hers, but the tone of official statements alluded to Ms Zacharia being sacked. "Katie's been treated very badly by the media. Very, very badly. Very unfairly, I think. And I just spoke to her about it. I said, Katie, is this for you?" he told reporters. "Because, you know, she's been treated very rough," he added. "And she's a nice person. Very nice person. I've watched her on television for years. But I said, is this for you, Katie? "You don't need this. You don't have to be treated. I would say the fake news, but just generally, the media has been very rough." Mr Trump recounted her appearance on Sean Hannity on Thursday. He said he saw the interview on Friday morning and said, "She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily." Mr Trump also told Ms Zacharia, "You don't have to do this if you don't want to." "I said to her, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider'," he said. "You think about it. But I would reconsider. She's got a beautiful husband and family. I met the family yesterday. Beautiful kids. It's like a picture postcard." The White House, when asked by The Mirror US for comment, pointed to a tweet reading, "A senior White House official tells @pdoocy Katie ZACHARIA is 'transitioning out' of the press secretary position." Ms Zacharia announced her departure from the White House in a post on X. "President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man," she wrote. "I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to," she added. "It was an honour to work for him."
news.summary: US President Donald Trump fired his new press secretary Katie Zacharia after five days in the job, leaving him without a spokesperson just weeks before the country's midterm elections
news.author: Tannur Anders

news.title: Trump Humiliated in Bombshell Crypto Lawsuit
news.text:
Donald Trump was sued Thursday by a cryptocurrency company that claims he violated the Constitution by profiting from deals with a United Arab Emirates official while in office.

Filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, the lawsuit names the 80-year-old president, his longtime friend and special envoy Steve Witkoff, and World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture co-founded by Trump’s family, accusing them of “corruptly profiting” from more than $2 billion in deals.

“No president in American history has profited from his office so brazenly,” said the lawsuit, filed by a shareholder of Circle Internet Group.

“The President himself has openly admitted that the lack of consequences emboldens him, not only to continue using his high office to enrich himself, but to expand the fortune he is extracting from the trust the American people placed in him.”

The plaintiff is Joel Greenberg, a shareholder in Circle, a publicly traded crypto company that competes with World Liberty Financial.

At the heart of the lawsuit, Greenberg alleges that Trump is violating the Constitution’s Foreign Emoluments Clause by profiting from a foreign government without congressional approval.

Greenberg also alleges that Trump diverted business away from Circle by accepting hundreds of millions of dollars, harming the company’s shareholders.

Four days before Trump’s inauguration, for example, the Trump family sold 49 percent of World Liberty Financial for $500 million to an investment entity backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE’s national security adviser, the lawsuit states. Financial disclosures confirmed this purchase after he became president.

“Millions of dollars from that deal, routed from a foreign government, flowed to President Trump after he assumed office,” the suit alleged.

The suit also claims Tahnoon orchestrated a scheme to inflate the value of Trump’s crypto holdings. It points to MGX, a UAE government-created investment fund Tahnoon chairs, which announced a $2 billion investment in the crypto exchange Binance just weeks after Trump took office.

World Liberty Financial then announced the launch of its own stablecoin, USD1, which MGX used to pay for the Binance deal.

“The President brazenly violated the Constitution in order to enrich himself, his family, and his business, at a direct cost to Circle. He needs to be held accountable,” Greenberg said in a statement provided to the Daily Beast.

A White House spokesperson did not immediately respond to questions from the Daily Beast.

Trump later made headlines for pardoning Changpeng Zhao, the billionaire founder of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, who was convicted of money laundering.

news.title: Judge delivers stunner as Trump faces major blow right before Christmas
news.text:
President Donald Trump just suffered a humiliation in court as he continues to litigate his defeat six years ago in the 2020 election.

"President Donald Trump must sit for a deposition two weeks before Christmas in his $10 billion defamation case against the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) or risk having the lawsuit thrown out, presenting him with a familiar choice," reported Matt Naham from Law and Crime on Thursday.

"U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett issued the Dec. 11 deadline after BBC attorneys accused the president of deliberately stalling, The Associated Press reported," he added. "The BBC's lawyers emphasized that Trump skipped a previously scheduled Oct. 16 deposition, citing "matters of national importance," only to attend a political campaign event in Georgia instead."

The lawsuit stems from BBC airing a documentary called "Trump: A Second Chance" in late 2025 about Trump that implied he directly called for violent action during his Jan. 6 speech. The BBC denies Trump's defamation accusation.

Trump has suffered a number of humiliating legal setbacks during his presidency. He lost 26 consecutive court cases in attempts to force states to give him their voter rolls, presumably so his immigration and other voter fraud authorities could detect undocumented immigrants and other would-be voters.

In July, he was embarrassed when he attempted to sue The New York Times for exposing details about the jet he purchased from Qatar.

“The Times swiftly moved to quash the subpoenas, arguing that they were issued in a bad faith effort to harass and intimidate the journalists,” Lawfare's Anna Bower reported at the time. “What’s more, the newspaper contended that the government hadn't come close to meeting the standard set out in New York Times v. Gonzales, the Second Circuit precedent establishing that prosecutors seeking a reporter's confidential sources must show, among other things, that the information can't be obtained by other means.”

Bower continued, “The Justice Department, in response, didn't ask the court to deny the motion outright. Instead, it asked the court to hold the subpoenas in abeyance for two weeks while it pursued additional investigative steps—steps that, the government suggested, might bear on the scope of the subpoenas and on whether the Gonzales factors could ultimately be satisfied.”

The judge in the case, Justice Arun Subramanian, blasted the government for failing to live up the Gonzalez precedent. This also happened with Judge Ana Reyes, who earlier on Thursday was profiled for her frequent clashing with Trump, including over his allegedly unauthorized destruction of public land to renovate the East Potomac Golf Course.

"Judge Ana Reyes of the US District Court for the District of Columbia is the latest judge to find herself in the crosshairs of an administration that’s escalated tensions with the federal judiciary and targeted individual judges who’ve ruled against its agenda," reported Bloomberg's Suzanne Monk earlier on Thursday.

She continued, "The judge’s refusal to tolerate perceived missteps by the Justice Department are part and parcel with her approach on the bench, where she’s known to be direct with litigants and quick to criticize shoddy courtroom behavior."

When discussing Trump's golf course actions, Reyes wrote that "for months, the Court has declined Plaintiffs’ repeated requests to restrain the Government’s activities at East Potomac Golf Course. Time and again, it has credited Government counsel’s representations and refused to presume bad faith. The Government now seeks to disqualify the Court for bias. That is a serious charge. The Court answers it. With the record."
