news.title: France braces for fresh unrest as Macron restricts protests and Paris shopkeepers arm themselves
news.text: French authorities continued preparations Thursday evening for a major day of nationwide protests planned for Saturday by groups opposing the country's economic conditions, exactly one week after the previous wave of demonstrations on October 17 descended into widespread violence. During those riots, crowds attacked police officers and government buildings and looted hundreds of shops and businesses across France. President Emmanuel Macron announced that authorities would prohibit demonstrations organized by what he called "illegitimate" groups, referring to far-left organizations that the government blames for last weekend's unrest. Marseille and Lyon, France's second- and third-largest cities, have both announced blanket bans on demonstrations within their jurisdictions Saturday. However, activists may challenge the restrictions in court, arguing that they violate their constitutionally protected right to protest. The calls for nationwide demonstrations are being led by France's main student union, UNEF, and members of the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged during protests against the rising cost of living and Macron's economic policies in 2018. Fearing another outbreak of widespread violence, Macron's government has promised a "massive deployment" of police officers. The administration acknowledged that it had been inadequately prepared for the previous demonstrations, when nearly 1 million people took to the streets, far exceeding official estimates. Some military personnel will also assist, including soldiers from Operation Sentinelle, the counterterrorism force deployed to patrol French cities following the wave of Islamic State terrorist attacks in France and elsewhere in Europe beginning in 2015. The soldiers will secure sensitive sites, freeing additional police officers to manage demonstrations and prevent looting. Authorities in Paris also attempted to prevent demonstrations Thursday over concerns that they could turn violent, but a court overturned the police ban. Thousands subsequently gathered in the capital for a stationary protest rather than the march originally planned. No major incidents were reported. One sign carried by demonstrators read: "We don't need tear gas for our future to look bleak." Meanwhile, Macron convened a special security meeting at the Élysée Palace, where he again accused far-left organizations of orchestrating last weekend's riots in an effort to create anarchy in France. "Last Saturday, we witnessed political and subversive acts by far-left groups whose objective is to bring down the republic," Macron said. The president explained that the government's strategy for the coming days would be to reject demonstration requests submitted by "individuals or groups without legitimate authorization." "The rules are simple, and I think they are simply a matter of common sense," he said. "The general recommendation is that no demonstrations take place in the coming days. For those who nevertheless wish to demonstrate, if they are trade unions, prefects will propose alternative routes." Macron was referring to routes considered less dangerous for business owners, many of whom fear further looting. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin called for tough measures against anyone violating protest bans, including stripping offenders of their voting rights. He also proposed restricting social media access for people involved in violence, looting or attacks on police officers. In recent days, relative calm has returned to Paris and other French cities, partly following the introduction of partial curfews. On Thursday evening, authorities in the capital announced an extension of the nighttime curfew covering the Place de la République area and the Les Halles district, from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. local time, until Monday morning. The French Culture Ministry also announced that several of Paris' most prominent museums, including the Louvre and Musée d'Orsay, would remain closed Saturday. The Grand Palais, Picasso Museum and Musée de l'Orangerie will also close for the day. The ministry instructed institutions under its supervision to take all necessary measures to ensure "visitor safety," "employee protection" and "the preservation of works of art." Organizers of Art Basel Paris, the international art fair, also announced that the event would be closed over the weekend. Paris City Hall urged residents and visitors to "exercise the utmost vigilance" Saturday because of "the risk of further violence by rioters who have no connection to the social protest movement." Shopkeepers across the capital are also preparing for renewed unrest. Last weekend's riots damaged 450 businesses in Paris alone, with 228 of them looted. Many owners have begun boarding up storefront windows with wooden panels in an attempt to protect their premises against break-ins and theft. Along Boulevard de Magenta, which connects Gare de l'Est railway station with Place de la République, workers spent Thursday installing protective boards over shopfronts. There, as elsewhere in the city, the makeshift barriers have also become gathering points for efforts to support local businesses. One poster urged residents to join a neighborhood WhatsApp group intended, among other things, to "prevent break-ins." Another called for donations to a fund supporting "Ali Hussein and his devastated team" after their shop was looted. French news agency AFP reported that growing fears of further violence have also prompted many Paris business owners to purchase weapons for self-defense. Yves Goulet, who owns a gun shop in Paris, told AFP that sales had "increased tenfold" since the riots and that he had already sold out of guns that fire rubber bullets. According to Goulet, shopkeepers are "arming themselves because they are terrified," while some customers told him they had been "trapped inside their stores with the looters." Michael, a Paris optician whose name was changed to protect his identity, purchased pepper spray from another weapons shop. He said he bought it "in case looters enter the store," explaining that it would give him at least "some measure of protection." Other business owners told AFP they hoped authorities would be better prepared this time and prevent another breakdown of law and order. "Last Saturday was a nightmare. I was afraid I would be killed," said hairstylist José Gedge. "But I refuse to believe for even a moment that this Saturday will look the same." Gedge expressed confidence that authorities had "learned lessons" from the previous unrest. He spoke to reporters in front of his salon's glass door, which had been smashed by rioters and temporarily repaired with wooden boards that still allowed cold air to blow inside. Emmanuel Renal, 60, who owns a paint and home improvement supply store near Gare de l'Est, remains traumatized by last weekend's events. Since Monday, he has been sleeping inside his shop, which is now half empty. "I doubt we'll be open next Saturday," he said. "I still don't understand why the looters came to steal paint and tools." Last weekend's riots began after large demonstrations against the rising cost of living and deteriorating conditions in educational institutions. The protests were largely led by radical left-wing activists and included significant participation from immigrant communities. Rioters attacked police officers and threw stones at them, assaulted passersby, set fire to garbage bins, cars and buildings, and looted or damaged approximately 3,000 businesses in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Nice, Nantes, Limoges and numerous other cities. More than 2,700 people were arrested during the unrest, and nearly 1,000 police officers were injured, some seriously. Macron and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu acknowledged intelligence and preparedness failures that left police overwhelmed by the scale of the violence. The demonstrations that preceded the riots brought together high school and university students, trade unions and members of the Yellow Vest movement. They followed weeks of student protests that began last month in schools in impoverished suburbs north of Paris, driven by teacher shortages and poor educational conditions. Those demonstrations were also marked by numerous violent incidents, and similar unrest subsequently spread to other European countries, including Belgium. In France and abroad, some commentators have emphasized the involvement of immigrants and the children of immigrants from Africa, Arab countries and Muslim-majority nations in both the demonstrations and the violence. Such allegations have circulated since the student protests earlier this month. U.S. President Donald Trump also claimed that the unrest was evidence of an alleged attempt by Islam to take over France. Macron rejected those claims, calling them an "absolute lie," and has instead emphasized the role of far-left organizations in the riots. Prime Minister Lecornu, along with right-wing figures in France, has accused Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, of allegedly fueling the violence as a show of political strength ahead of next year's presidential election. Polls cited in the report project that Mélenchon would reach the decisive second round against far-right leader Marine Le Pen but would then lose by a wide margin.
news.summary: After riots left nearly 1,000 police officers injured and 3,000 businesses damaged or looted, France prepares a massive security deployment for Saturday's demonstrations; Paris museums will close, curfews remain in place and protest bans face legal challenges

news.title: Trump blasts 76ers star LeBron James as 'disgrace' for not standing still during national anthem
news.text:
Trump blasts 76ers star LeBron James as 'disgrace' for not standing still during national anthem

Trump blasts LeBron James

President Donald Trump on Thursday accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the NBA star appeared to continue his warmups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia’s season opener on Tuesday.

“I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video. “LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!”

James appeared to practice a golf swing and jump shot as “The Star-Spangled Banner” was performed Tuesday at New York's Madison Square Garden. James, starting his first season with Philadelphia, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem.

Trump and James have been critical of each other for years, occasionally trading public swipes.

The 41-year-old James, in his record 24th NBA season, made his home debut for the Sixers Thursday night against Cleveland, and he did not comment publicly or post on social media about Trump's gripe before the game.

James put his arms behind his back and bowed his head while Boyz II Men sang the anthem ahead of the opener. James was introduced to a roaring ovation from the crowd of roughly 20,000.

Coach Nick Nurse had talked at length since training camp opened about the Sixers' need to tune out outside distractions. Hours before their home opener, the Sixers had to deal with one from the president.

“I think that goes right in with other outside noise we've already had,” Nurse said before the game. “I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor. The focus that they've had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding.”

Among some of the more notable times James became entangled with the president or politics:

LeBron wears 1 black shoe, 1 white shoe

James was with Cleveland in 2017 when he made a statement with his shoes — one black, one white, with the word “equality” in capital gold letters on the back of each.

Then, after the game, James made a statement about Trump, saying: “This is a beautiful country and we’re never going to let one person dictate how beautiful and how powerful we are.”

James had called Trump “ a bum ” on Twitter and also said earlier that season of the president: “He doesn’t understand how many kids, no matter the race, look up to the president of the United States for guidance, for leadership, for words of encouragement. He doesn’t understand that, and that’s what makes me more sick than anything.”

Shut up and dribble

James showed determination to speak out on social issues and the nation’s political climate after Fox News host Laura Ingraham criticized the four-time NBA champion for his 2018 comments about social issues.

“We will definitely not shut up and dribble,” James said. “I will definitely not do that. I mean too much to society. I mean too much to the youth. I mean too much to so many kids that feel like they don’t have a way out and they need someone to help lead them out of the situation they’re in.”

James referenced Muhammad Ali, Jim Brown, Bill Russell and Jackie Robinson as athletes who previously spoke up for equality and change with no concerns about the consequences or any rewards.

“We know it’s bigger than us,” James said.

Response to Morey's tweet about Hong Kong

James said in 2019 that former Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey “was either misinformed or not really educated on the situation” regarding the potential consequences of his actions when he tweeted in support of Hong Kong’s pro-democracy protests.

“Yes, we do have freedom of speech,” James said. “But at times, there are ramifications for the negative that can happen when you’re not thinking about others, when you only think about yourself. I don’t want to get into a word or sentence feud with Daryl Morey, but I believe he wasn’t educated on the situation at hand, and he spoke.”

Morey deleted the tweet, but it nonetheless sparked a rift with the Chinese government, which severed ties with the NBA for several years.

Get people to the polls

James was named The Associated Press’ Male Athlete of the Year in 2020 in large part for leading the Los Angeles Lakers to a championship and helping to persuade many — at the peak of the Black Lives Matter movement — who had never voted to finally head to the polls.

“I still know what I do on the floor and obviously, I give everything to the game,” James said. “But I can make a greater impact off the floor right now, more than I can on the floor. And I want to continue to inspire people with the way I play the game of basketball. But there’s so many more things that I can do off the floor to help cultivate people, inspire people, bring people together, empower them.”

James rejects Ibrahimovic's criticism of activist athletes

AC Milan striker and former LA Galaxy star Zlatan Ibrahimovic blasted socially conscious athletes in a 2021 interview. Ibrahimovic called it “a mistake” for James and other athletes to get involved in political causes, saying they should “just do what you do best, because it doesn’t look good.”

James, naturally, rejected the criticism.

“I would never shut up about things that are wrong,” James said.
